News.title: Man 'crushed' in horror accident as police probe death in industrial yard
News.content:
Man 'crushed' in horror accident as police probe death in industrial yard

Steven Dougall, of Falkirk, died in hospital after the industrial accident at the yard operated by his family's Horizon Reinforcing & Crane Hire Co. Ltd

View 2 Images Steven Dougall died in an industrial accident (Image: HANDOUT)

A 21-year-old man has died after allegedly being crushed while working at an industrial yard.

‌



Steven Dougall, of Falkirk, died in hospital after the incident on July 21 at the yard operated by Horizon Reinforcing & Crane Hire Co. Ltd - his family's business.

‌



Tributes have poured in for Steven who has been described as a "hardworking, kind-hearted young man" and a balloon release memorial has been held in Dollar Park.

‌



Police Scotland said the circumstances are not being treated as suspicious but it is investigating the incident along with the Health and Safety Executive (HSE).

View 2 Images Balloon's released in Stephen's memory (Image: HANDOUT)

A force spokeswoman said: “Around 9.55am on Tuesday, 21 July, 2026, we were called to a report of a man seriously injured at an industrial premises on Castle Drive in Falkirk.

‌



“Emergency services attended and a 21-year-old man was taken to Forth Valley Royal Hospital in Larbert by ambulance where he died a short time later. His family is aware.

“The death is not being treated as suspicious however enquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances. The Health and Safety Executive has been made aware.” An HSE spokesman said: “We are aware and assisting Police Scotland with their enquiries.”

Over the last two weeks, tributes have flooded in for Steven with his family and the wider local community devastated by his sudden passing. Hundreds attended the release of balloons in his honour in Dollar Park last Tuesday, reported the Daily Record.

‌



An obituary posted online said: “The Falkirk community is mourning the heartbreaking loss of Steven Dougall, whose passing at the age of 21 has left his family, friends and loved ones devastated.

“Tributes shared in his memory reflect the profound impact he had on those around him and the deep sense of loss felt by everyone who knew him.

“Steven is being remembered as a hardworking, kind-hearted young man with ambitious goals and a bright future ahead of him… those closest to Steven remember him for his warm personality, infectious sense of humour, determination, and ability to create lasting memories with family and friends.”

Article continues below

It added his family has “requested privacy as they mourn their beloved son, grandson, cousin and friend”.

A keen amateur footballer, Steven’s life was also celebrated in a memorial match last week staged by Pantry FC, the local Monday league 6-a-side team he played for. The team posted: “Steven Dougall was the heart of Pantry and great friends with everyone involved, nobody was as competitive and infectious as him when it came to football in any form.

“The sudden loss of Steven has hurt everyone so deeply… We’d like to thank everyone who took part in this and especially all those who came to watch the game and support the boys in playing this match for Steven. It meant the world to those playing and to Steven’s family to see how many people turned out for him.”

News.title: Inside Britain’s cyber battlefield of the future as AI reshapes fighting
News.content:
Dawn had just broken over California’s Mojave desert but the heat was gathering and turning the distant mountains into a trembling blur.

Dust clung to boots, weapons and vehicles. The air smelled of diesel, scorched earth and hot metal. Then a British soldier stepped from a concealed position with a small controller in his hands.

Above him, almost invisible, an unmanned aircraft circled. On a screen below, enemy positions appeared as moving dots and live images. Coordinates were passed. Targets were confirmed. Seconds later, munitions fell behind hostile lines in ground too dangerous for any soldier to reach.

Sirens signalled a direct hit and casualties. Survivors dropped to their knees, tightening tourniquets around wounded comrades and carrying out emergency treatment in the dust.

‌



Before they had finished, driverless trucks and desert buggies were surging across the battlefield carrying water, ammunition, equipment and reinforcements.

No drivers. No pilots. No shouted orders carried down a trench.

View 6 Images A drone above the Mojave Desert, feeding live intelligence on enemy positions to troops below. (Image: Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID)

The Mirror joined British and allied troops at the US Army’s National Training Centre at Fort Irwin to witness the wars to come – in which artificial intelligence will watch from above, sift intelligence, guide vehicles and determine where and when troops strike.

‌



The machines may not yet be in command, but they are becoming the eyes, ears and nervous system of the battlefield.

This was Project Convergence-Capstone 6 (PC-C6) involving the Five Eyes alliance of Britain, the United States, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

In temperatures up to 49C, soldiers tested how they would fight an enemy armed with drones, cyber weapons, signal jammers and AI systems.

View 6 Images British soldiers take part in the vast Five Eyes exercise at Fort Irwin, testing how troops and artificial intelligence could fight side by side. (Image: Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID)

‌



The familiar image of troops advancing behind tanks while commanders study paper maps is being overtaken by something faster, more connected and potentially more deadly.

A drone can spot a target beyond the horizon. AI can examine streams of video, intercepted signals and battlefield data in moments.

A commander can launch a strike before an enemy realises it has been found. The aim is to compress decisions that take hours into seconds.

Yet senior officers insist that the machines are not being allowed to choose who lives and dies.

‌



View 6 Images Colonel Jim Howard said AI would make soldiers faster, more effective and more lethal while keeping humans in control of battlefield decisions.

None of the gear being tested was fully autonomous, according to Colonel Jim Howard, commander of the British Army’s Experimentation and Trials Group. He told the Mirror: “You allow AI to do the science, and the human to do the art. You’re not looking at replacing people, you are augmenting and accelerating people, and giving them the tools to be faster and better, and more lethal.”

The machine finds patterns, processes data and points towards danger. The human makes the judgment and gives the order. But the balance is shifting.

A soldier may still pull the trigger, yet AI could increasingly determine what they see.

‌



Col. Howard said that if an enemy can be located and struck before British soldiers are exposed, fewer lives are placed in danger. But there is another threat.

Every drone, sensor, vehicle and communication system depends on software. An enemy that can hack or jam that network could blind an entire force, stop its vehicles or feed commanders false information.

A modern army could become almost powerless if their digital web is torn apart. British teams, therefore, attacked their own gear, trying to disrupt signals. Col. Howard said: “All capabilities went through electronic warfare attack and jamming, to see how resilient they are. Some are able to shrug it off – there’s some very clever tech.”

View 6 Images Vehicles race carrying supplies, equipment and reinforcements into areas considered too dangerous for human drivers. (Image: Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID)

‌



At Fort Irwin, up to 60 pieces of gear were pushed through the dust and heat, including acoustic sensors, aerial drones and unmanned ground vehicles.

Col. Howard said: “There are technologies in that tent you could buy tomorrow. Others are more emergent and are going to require a bit more work,”

British troops were inserted into a US corps-level operation and required to connect their equipment with systems used by all five allied nations. Brigadier Karen Peek, the UK task force commander for PC-C6, said no country could face the emerging threat alone: “It is more complex than ever, and technology is evolving at a rapid rate. Making sure that we train as we would fight is really important.”

View 6 Images Mirror writer Jeremiah Hassel tries out the technology helping soldiers identify threats, process intelligence and direct operations on tomorrow’s battlefield. (Image: Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID)

‌



Fighting an enemy they cannot see or hear, armies that cannot communicate or move quickly enough may be destroyed before they know what is happening.

Yet Brig. Peek said the most important achievement was not found inside any tech: “This exercise is about way more; it’s about people, and building that trust. The allies are learning, adapting, innovating, and we are much more ready now for future challenges.”

The soldiers remain at the centre of the fight. They still carry the weapons and make the final decisions. But all around them, largely unseen, AI is already beginning to dominate the battlefield.

News.title: One in 10 Brits haven't had a bath in over a decade as UK bathing habits shift
News.content:
One in 10 Brits haven't had a bath in over a decade as UK bathing habits shift

A new survey of 2,000 adults shows one in 10 Brits haven't taken a bath in more than a decade, with over half saying bathing has fallen out of fashion as shower vs bath preferences shift across the UK.

View 3 Images A fifth of people no longer have a bath in their home (Image: Getty Images)

One in 10 Brits haven't had a bath in over a decade, new research has revealed. A survey of 2,000 adults found 51% believe bathing has become outdated. Nearly half (48%) now favour a shower, while 18% of people don't even have a bath in their homes. Others (14%) made this change specifically to help cut their water usage.

‌



Recent studies, including the Shower Market Report , have recorded a rise in renovations being carried out to remove disused baths. A fifth of people have had a bath taken out of their homes in a bid to create a bigger shower space (43%), modernise their bathroom (42%), or convert to a walk-in shower (31%).

‌



View 3 Images Nearly half believe baths have gone out of fashion (Image: Getty Images)

‌



A spokesperson from leading smart Pay-As-You-Go energy supplier Utilita, which commissioned the research to support its award winning High5 tips series , including to keep showers to four minutes maximum, said: "Once a staple of the home, baths seem to have fallen out of favour for many across the UK.

"From homes getting smaller to costs getting higher, there are numerous reasons why this might be. But however you choose to clean and refresh, the most important thing is being conscious about your water usage, for the sake of both your pocket and the planet."

A fifth of those without a bath cite a lack of time to unwind, while 33% are too impatient for the time they take to run. Other reasons for the drop in popularity included not wanting to use excessive water for either cost-saving or environmental purposes, with 77% describing themselves as mindful of the amount of water they use.

‌



View 3 Images Three quarters are mindful of the amount of water they use (Image: Getty Images)

Nine in 10 (90%) take deliberate steps to cut their water consumption, such as only filling the kettle with the water they need (55%), collecting rain to water plants (29%), limiting hosepipe use (29%), and re-using grey water (13%).

More than a third (35%) have ditched baths for showers for precisely this reason. Three quarters (76%) also believe this makes a difference to lowering their water bills, with 77% saying the same about taking shorter showers.

‌



Three in 10 (32%) said knowing exactly how much money they could save or seeing real-time costs per minute (30%) would persuade them to cut down.

Utilita's spokesperson added: "Swapping baths for showers or reducing the time spent doing either can be a small, easy change that can have a lasting impact.

"It's great to see so many people are already doing this and have faith in the money they could save on their bills from this simple act.

Article continues below

"And no matter whether you prefer baths or showers, everyone can be a water-savvy person."

News.title: Electric blue sea creatures wash up on UK beaches as experts issue warning
News.content:
Electric blue sea creatures wash up on UK beaches as experts issue warning

More stunning Velella Velella have been found on a beach in Cumbria, but marine experts have told people to look and not touch the creatures dubbed "alien jellyfish"

View 3 Images Velella velella and closely related to the Portuguese man o' war (Image: Curt Anstey)

The scorching heatwaves this summer have enticed Brits to the seaside.

‌



But they've also attracted hundreds of these incredible creatures too.

‌



Hundreds of the electric blue animals, thought to be Velella Velella, also known as by-the-wind sailors, have been found washed up on our sand since the temperatures rocketed.

‌



Visitors to St Bees beach in Cumbria spotted several over the weekend, while hundreds were found on the Welsh coast at the start of the summer.

The animals are closely related to the Portuguese Man o’ War, stings from which can cause nasty welts and even death in rare cases. Though the Velella Velella are understood to be less dangerous, it is warned not to touch them.

View 3 Images Beachgoers have been urged not to touch the blue creatures by marine experts (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

‌



One of world's most dangerous sea creatures washes up in popular holiday spot READ MORE :

They are usually found in the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans but temperatures over here have rocketed to nearly 40C in recent weeks. It remains warm, with 27.8C recorded in Charlwood, Surrey, on Saturday, but an unsettled period is expected this week.

Nevertheless, experts believe beachgoers will see more of the electric blue creatures this summer. Beachgoers who have encountered them so far expressed their surprise. Louise Nicholson mistook one for seaweed at St Bees beach recently.

Speaking to BBC Cumbria, she said: "There were hundreds of them and there were lots of visitors to the area taking photos. They are absolutely beautiful, only about 2ins in size. It was a great find on a beautiful day."

‌



Marine biologists say the creatures, sometimes dubbed "alien jellyfish", are usually seen elsewhere in autumn and winter.

Georgia de Jong Cleyndert, Head of Marine at the Cumbria Wildlife Trust, said: "Although they are not jellyfish, they do have a very mild sting, even after they have washed up so do not touch them.

"Each by-the-wind sailor is made up of hundreds of tiny, specialised animals working together as a single floating colony."

‌



View 3 Images Beaches, like this one at Margate, Kent, have been busy with tourists recently (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire)

Marine specialist Frankie Hobro, owner of Anglesey Sea Zoo in Bynsiencyn, said their sting is generally "very mild" in comparison to Portuguese man o' war - but also said it was unwise to touch them.

"You probably wouldn't feel it through normal fingers because human skin is fairly thick," she said.

‌



"But if you touched your lips, face or another sensitive area, it could be quite painful and cause a tingling sensation. I would always recommend covering up when in the sea.

“By-the-wind-sailors are not dangerous but their stings can irritate and you wouldn’t want to touch your face or eyes if you’ve been in contact with one.

“We’ll soon be seeing reports of more dangerous creatures like Weever fish and Portuguese Man o’War. It can be difficult to avoid contacts but a rash vest will help and swim socks or booties are good idea."

Article continues below

Electric blue by-the-wind-sailors are “colonial hydroids” – meaning they’re not a single creature but are made up of a colony of tiny individual animals, and re not true jellyfish.

“What is slightly worrying is that Portuguese Man o’ War are arriving earlier in the year and more frequently, overlapping with marine creatures like By-the-wind-sailors. It shows how climate change is affecting ocean currents." Hobro added.

News.title: Andy Burnham vows to be 'relentless' on small boats crisis - and aims a dig at his rivals
News.content:
Andy Burnham vows to be 'relentless' on small boats crisis - and aims a dig at his rivals

Andy Burnham pledged to get a grip on the numbers of people making the perilous Channel crossing - but said safe routes were needed to tackle vile smuggling gangs

View 3 Images Andy Burnham visited HM Coastguard Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre, in Dover, as he pledged to grip the small boats crisis (Image: Jack Taylor/PA Wire)

Andy Burnham has said he will be relentless in tackling small boat arrivals as he took a veiled swipe at his right-wing opponents for playing politics.

‌



The Prime Minister pledged to get a grip on the numbers of people making the perilous Channel crossing, but said safe routes were needed to tackle the business model used by vile smuggling gangs.

‌



On a visit to Dover, Mr Burnham pointed to a sharp fall in crossings, with the number of arrivals at this point in the year 43% lower than last year. The provisional total for this year is 14,526, compared to 25,436 last summer.

‌



The PM said: "Clearly, progress is being made, but we’re not complacent. We’re just going to be relentless. People want to see this issue addressed. I heard that on the doorsteps in Makerfield."

Small boat driver who filmed himself steering dangerously overcrowded vessel jailed READ MORE :

View 3 Images Andy Burnham and Border Security Minister Anna Turley stand by a recovered small boat, which was used by migrants crossing the English Channel (Image: Jack Taylor/PA Wire)

He added: "But we also need to build a system that offers safe routes for people as well, because that also takes away the selling point of the gangs. So on every level we’ve got to cover this … crucially increasing the enforcement activity.”

‌



Reform and the Tories have both seized on the issue of small boat crossings, with Nigel Farage's regularly stoking fears about an "invasion" of migrants.

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp has spent the start of the summer recess filming videos about small boats - which turned farcical when he accused a French warship of firing 17 "live rounds" to intimidate him as he filmed an interview in the Channel.

Asked if he wanted to change the tone of the debate, Mr Burnham said: “We have to deal with the issue rather than play politics with the issue. Just deal with it head on, grip it, and then make the changes that will bring that reassurance to the public.

‌



“The public don’t like the idea that the border looks like it’s not controlled. We need to bring back that control, but also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it.

“It’s about changing the whole approach, and slowly but surely we are putting in place those building blocks of a very different approach to this issue. It’s working, but there’s more to be done.”

At least 13 people are believed to have died trying to cross the Channel so far this year - with four lives lost in 24 hours last week.

‌



One man died after a boat capsized off France's northern coast on Wednesday, and a one-year-old child was hurt. Three people were found dead onboard a boat that had launched from Dunkirk on the French coast.

View 3 Images Three migrants died on Thursday (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire)

Mr Burnham visited Dover’s joint command room, where officers from the National Crime Agency (NCA), Maritime and Coastguard Agency and the Border Security Command track movements across the Channel using surveillance drones.

‌



He was shown a small boat used by 96 migrants in May this year, along with a surveillance drone used to detect small boat activity.

Meanwhile, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood visited NCA headquarters in Stratford as the Government said the numbers of officers tackling organised immigration crime has more than doubled from 376 to almost 800.

Ms Mahmood said the plans to tackle small boat crossing were starting to "bear fruit" but said she was determined to crack down on the factors pulling people to make the journey.

‌



She said: “I want to change the calculus. I want them to change their mind about whether they get on the boat in the first place.”

Ms Mahmood has announced a string of measures to discourage people coming to the UK, including a controversial proposal to make refugee status temporary.

It comes as the latest figures showed 326 people arrived on Saturday in four boats, bringing the number of people crossing the strait to 2,057 since Mr Burnham became PM on July 20.

Article continues below

Wednesday was the busiest day for small boat crossings so far this year, with 752 migrants arriving in the UK.

Numbers tend to fluctuate due to changes in the weather, with peaks in the summer months, according to the Home Office.

News.title: Man arrested in major update after British woman found dead in suitcase
News.content:
Man arrested in major update after British woman found dead in suitcase

The body of Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, from the Edinburgh area, was discovered inside a suitcase by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of Athens

View 2 Images The body of Elisabeth-Jane Ross was found in a suitcase (Image: Facebook)

A man has been arrested following the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found inside a suitcase in Athens.

The body of Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, from the Edinburgh area, was discovered by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of Athens on July 18. She is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found.

And now a 26-year-old man, who Greek police said was a foreigner, has been arrested.

During the period from when she is thought to have died until Ms Ross' body was found, someone was reportedly using her mobile phone to send messages purporting to be from her.

View 2 Images Elisabeth-Jane Ross died in Athens (Image: Facebook)

Hellenic Police, Greece’s national force, have said they were able to identify the victim using fingerprints. Earlier this week, toxicology tests were being carried out to establish if "foul play" was involved in her death and a cause of death has not yet been given.

Ms Ross entered Greece on June 26 and was initially staying with friends in Piraeus. She is then said to have gone to meet with American friends in another part of the Greek capital, but it is unclear if this ever happened.

The Hellenic Police said they analysed video footage to identify the suspect, who confessed on Thursday. The 26-year-old man is believed to have put her body into a suitcase, taking it to the abandoned site where it was found.

In the following days he is said to have used her bank card to withdraw money. A replica pistol and a knife were found at the suspect’s home and police have filed a case against him for manslaughter, robbery and violation of weapons laws.

Previously a spokesperson for the Greek police, Konstantina Dimoglidou, said: "Our priority is to get to the bottom of who left the suitcase. Whoever they were was careful not to leave fingerprints or DNA.

"We've had the entire homicide division of the Greek FBI working on the case. We're in contact with other police forces. We're going to solve this."

The Foreign and Commonwealth Office said earlier: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”

Article continues below

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece. Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”

News.title: Andy Burnham backs Mirror water safety campaign as drownings spike in hot weather
News.content:
Andy Burnham backs Mirror water safety campaign as drownings spike in hot weather

EXCLUSIVE: Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was vital for people to understand the dangers of open water swimming and credited our 'Save Lives for Sam' campaign for raising awareness

The Prime Minister backs the Mirror's water safety campaign

Andy Burnham has thrown his weight behind the Mirror's water safety campaign after dozens of people lost their lives in a horrifying spate of drownings.

‌



The Prime Minister said it was vital that people understood the dangers of open water swimming and credited our 'Save Lives for Sam' campaign for raising awareness.

‌



Some 40 people have lost their lives after getting into difficulty in open water across the UK since May 24, with successive heatwaves driving people to seek respite from scorching temperatures.

‌



Mr Burnham joined the backers of the Mirror's campaign, named in memory of Sam Haycock, a 16-year-old boy who drowned in a reservoir in Rotherham, South Yorkshire, in 2021.

These are the faces of dozens of tragic Brits who lost their lives in open water READ MORE :

Water safety: Your complete guide to staying safe in the water on World Drowning Prevention Day READ MORE :

View 3 Images PM Andy Burnham has backed the Mirror's campaign for better water safety after dozens of people lost their lives in open water (Image: JASON ALDEN/POOL/EPA/Shutterstock)

The Prime Minister told us: "I do back your campaign, and I give great credit to The Mirror, so often a campaigning newspaper, but rightly so on this issue... It's really important that people understand the dangers of open water swimming, particularly if people are not regular swimmers, it can cause real issues.

‌



"Water safety measures around is part of it. It's also about making sure, as part of the curriculum, kids get the right swimming support, and that's I think a key part of the campaign.

"I really support what the Mirror are doing. I remember from my time as [Greater Manchester] Mayor when those incidents happen, they're so tragic."

He went on: "It's enticing sometimes to think of jumping in, but it's the coldness and the shock of that that makes people lose their breath and then struggle, and it can happen so quickly.

‌



"Credit to The Mirror; it's a really important campaign, and I would just ask everybody to listen to what you're calling for, make these changes, but also take great care. Enjoy the summer, but take great care."

The Mirror has joined forces with bereaved families and lifesaving charities to call for drowning to be treated as a national emergency. Olympic legends Becky Adlington and Tom Dean, and elite swimmer and TV presenter Michael Gunning have also given it their backing.

Our campaign calls for 'Sam's Law' to make it a legal requirement for safety equipment to be installed around high risk large bodies of water.

‌



Other demands include an urgent public awareness campaign, action to make it an aggravated criminal offence to damage or steal safety equipment, and pressure on water companies and those in control of high risk bodies of water to provide proper safety equipment. A Minister for Water Safety must also be appointed in England, as in Wales and Scotland.

Sam's dad, Simon Haycock said: "I'm over the moon that Andy Burnham has decided to back our campaign. Hopefully this will progress it and see it over the line.

"It's been relentless this summer, it just keeps coming and coming. It's really heart breaking. We need to keep the momentum going now."

‌



3 View 3 Images Sam Haycock, 16, died after jumping into a reservoir in 2021 (Image: Haycock family) 3 View 3 Images Joe Abbess, 17, drowned after getting caught in a rip current in 2023 (Image: Vanessa Abbess)

Vanessa Abbess, who has been campaigning in memory of her 17-year-old son Joe who drowned in a rip current in Bournemouth in 2023, said multiple drowning tragedies should be treated as a public health emergency.

‌



She said: "I am delighted to hear that Andy Burnham supports the Save Lives for Sam campaign. It is encouraging to hear that he understands the importance of water safety education.

"I hope he will act quickly to appoint a Water Safety Minister, who would lead the government's drowning prevention initiatives, with cross-sector collaboration and bereaved family support."

Save Lives for Sam - our demands Together, we are all calling for: The Government to launch an urgent public awareness campaign ahead of the summer holidays which targets parents and children on TikTok and other social media platforms. This should include lifesaving techniques and advice such as avoid diving into the water and information on cold water shock. Water companies and those in control of high risk large water bodies, to ‘do the right thing’ by bringing in the correct safety equipment. Compulsory lessons in schools (ahead of the holidays) on how to survive if you get into difficulty in the water, which should include the Water Safety Code, the RNLI ‘Float to Live’ campaign, and Phone-Float-Throw bystander advice. Put in place ‘Sam’s Law’. We urge the Government to make it law that safety equipment should be installed around high risk large bodies of water and make damaging this safety equipment an aggravated criminal offence to damage or steal this safety equipment. Currently it is already a criminal offence under theft or criminal damage but the penalties are low for these very minor offences. And finally the appointment of a Minister for Water Safety, as they have in Wales and Scotland, as drowning must be accepted as a preventable public health issue.

‌



She added: "Anyone can drown, no-one should, but I strongly believe through mass public service messaging and education, lives can be saved"

Ashley Jones, of the Royal Life Saving Society (RLSS UK), said: “RLSS UK is pleased to hear of the Prime Minister’s support for the campaign, and his recognition of water safety education and drowning prevention as important issues that need action to prevent future tragedies.

"Drowning is a preventable public health issue, and a broad systems approach is required to reduce the number of lives lost."

Article continues below

He called for schools to get proper funding to deliver swimming and water safety education in England, which has been pledged in Scotland and Wales.

He added: “We look forward to seeing action from the Government that follows up on the PM’s words. RLSS UK is keen to collaborate and together implement real change to save lives.”

News.title: Ghana Party in the Park organisers apologise after crush at entrance of family festival
News.content:
Ghana Party in the Park organisers apologise after crush at entrance of family festival

Police and ambulances were called to a London park after a Ghana Party in the Park descended into chaos - organisers have released a lengthy statement a "crowd surge"

View 3 Images A 'crowd surge' happened at the Ghana Party in the Park festival (Image: Plus 1 TV)

Organisers of a London festival where multiple people were left injured following a crush have apologised.

‌



Disturbing footage shared on social media shows guests screaming in terror and desperately trying to free themselves of the crowd surge at Ghana Party in the Park on Saturday. Some guests are seen falling to the floor and others are heard shouting in panic amid the chaotic scenes in the park in Barnet, north London.

‌



Three people were taken to hospital with others sustaining less serious injuries.. Now, the festival organisers have apologised and called the scenes "deeply upsetting".

‌



Witnesses saw injured people being carried from the grounds on stretchers by medics. One 18-year-old present described the incident as "very chaotic," adding that the festival was "very poorly organised".

View 3 Images Several people were left injured after the incident (Image: Plus 1 TV)

The official statement, posted on the event's Instagram page, said: "Yesterday was one of the most difficult days in the history of Ghana Party in the Park. First and foremost, our thoughts are with everyone who was injured, distressed or otherwise affected by the events that took place.

‌



"Seeing members of our community impacted in this way has been deeply upsetting. We sincerely apologise and our hearts go out to everyone involved. We wish those who sustained injuries a full and speedy recovery and extend our sincere support to their families, friends and loved ones."

But speculation on social media suggesting a stabbing had occured is inaccurate, both the festival and the Metropolitan Police confirmed. Nevertheless, following the crowd surge, the festival closed early on Saturday. Organisers said its thoughts are with those people injured and their families.

View 3 Images The festival took place at Copthall Playing Fields, in north London (Image: google maps)

‌



The statement added: " We are also aware of inaccurate information circulating on social media. We can confirm that there were no stabbing incidents at the festival and no fatalities occurred.

"Earlier in the day a fire involving a vendors [sic] required a temporary pause to the festival while the London Fire Brigade emergency services and our event safety teams responded. Once the incident had been addressed and the affected area declared safe normal event operations resumed.

"Later in the day a crowd surge at the festival entrance resulted in several attendees sustaining injuries. Emergency services responded immediately including the Metropolitan Police, London Ambulance Service, London Fire Brigade and the Air Ambulance. Following discussions with the emergency services and our events management company the difficult decision was taken to bring the festival to an early close in the interests of public safety.

‌



"For more than twenty years Ghana Party in the Park has celebrated Ghanaian culture, music and community, welcoming thousands of people in a safe and positive environment. This year's event was in conjunction with ShattaFest."

Following the incident, Met Police in Barnet said: "Officers are at Copthall Playing Fields where Ghana Party in the Park has been cancelled after an overcrowding issue at the entrance saw several people sustain non-life threatening injuries. Speculation about a stabbing is inaccurate. Please help us by avoiding the area."

"A total of 23 people received some form of assistance either from the emergency services or the event medical team, with nine people assessed by the London Ambulance Service.

Article continues below

"Three were taken to hospital, where their condition was confirmed as non-life-threatening. The event was ended early, and crowds left without further incident."

News.title: Burnham pledges to be 'relentless' in curbing small boat crossings
News.content:
Andy Burnham has pledged his government will be "relentless" in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats.

The prime minister said progress had been made and the government was "changing the whole approach", with enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs doubled on both sides of the Channel.

"People want to see this issue addressed," he said in Dover, adding: "We also need to build a system that offers safe routes for people as well, because that also takes away the selling point of the gangs."

Political discussions around the UK's policies on illegal migration have resurfaced since tens of thousands of migrants swam into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on Thursday.

Burnham noted that 98% of the people who swam to the African territory had been returned to Morocco - which he said had dealt with the immediate issue.

But he added: "There's a broader issue about the Schengen area and our relationship with it, and of course, I would want to be in regular dialogue with the EU on those issues."

His comments came shortly after the Home Office announced that the number of National Crime Agency (NCA) officers tackling smuggling gangs facilitating small boat crossings had risen to almost 800 from 376 at the start of 2025.

Burnham said there had been a similar doubling of French officers.

Asked whether he wanted to change the tone of the debate around small boats, he said that he wanted to "deal with the issue rather than play politics with the issue".

He added: "The public don't like the idea that the border looks like it's not controlled. We need to bring back that control. But also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it."

News.title: Man admits transporting Scottish woman's body in suitcase, Greek police say
News.content:
Greek police say a man has admitted transporting the body of a Scottish woman in a suitcase to an abandoned building.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, days after she was reported missing.

Local officers launched an investigation with cooperation from authorities in the US, the UK and Scotland, and now say they have arrested a 26-year-old man - the BBC understands he is from Afghanistan.

The force said he was brought to police headquarters on Thursday where he "confessed to his actions". He was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, robbery and weapons offences, but the exact charges have yet to be finalised under the Greek legal system.

News.title: Prolonged drought could cause shortage of some foods, farmers' union head says
News.content:
Bradshaw also suggested farmers should be given tax breaks to build water storage systems on their land to prepare for the years ahead.

"We have taken our food supply for granted for far too long," he added.

"Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well.

"It does feel like there is going be some shortages of [food] products", Bradshaw told Radio 4's Broadcasting House.

In a message to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, he said: "Let's draw a line in the sand and make sure we prioritise domestic food production to deliver growth across the UK."

After a wet and mild start to the year, it has been exceptionally dry hot and dry with a succession of heatwaves across the UK.

The combination of low rainfall and prolonged heat has quickly depleted water reserves in soils, vegetation and rivers.

While droughts can occur naturally, climate change is making weather patterns more erratic, and heatwaves more frequent and intense.

Scientists say there is a greater risk of droughts happening as a result, and of them being more severe and longer-lasting when they do.

The Met Office reports that England saw just 5.6mm of rainfall up to 30 July â just 8% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

For Wales it was 7.9mm of rainfall, also 8% of its long-term average for the month and almost a third of the previous record of 22.6mm, again set in 1911.

Heat health alerts are in place across most of England until at least 09:00 BST on Wednesday.

Amber alerts indicate a rise in deaths of vulnerable people and increased demand on health services are likely, while yellow alerts indicate these are possible.

News.title: Massive Attack responds after Singapore ban over Palestine display
News.content:
Massive Attack has said it was "surprised and disappointed" by its treatment by Singaporean authorities after expressing pro-Palestine sentiments during a performance in the city-state.

The group wrote on Instagram on Sunday that its members were "detained by the police, isolated and separately questioned", with some subject to hotel room searches and temporary passport confiscation.

The band's two members held up a Palestinian flag during its 29 July show there and shouted "free Palestine" alongside members of the audience.

Singapore, which has stringent rules on public speech and assembly, subsequently said it had indefinitely banned Massive Attack from returning to the country.

A police spokeswoman told the BBC on Friday that the two band members would not be allowed to re-enter Singapore and were barred from performing there.

Robert Del Naja and Grant Marshall were "given stern warnings" concerning alleged offences under two laws that restrict the public display of foreign flags and regulate political expressions at public events.

Massive Attack said that before the show and again at the end "large sections of the auditorium organically led chants of 'Free Palestine', presumably aware but undeterred that this spontaneous expression alone could violate their government's censorship laws".

The band did not address the ban directly, but described the situation as a "surreal experience" and said it "did not imagine that merely holding up the flag of a sovereign state recognised by 157 countries would violate any law".

It added that it was "proud to have made the impromptu expression" with fans in Singapore, who "clearly felt a moral imperative to show solidarity with the people of Palestine".

Massive Attack is known for openly expressing its political stance on a range of issues, including the war in Gaza.

Del Naja was arrested earlier this year on suspicion of showing support for the proscribed organisation Palestine Action during a protest in London.

The 61-year-old sat among hundreds of fellow demonstrators with a sign that read "I Oppose Genocide, I Support Palestine Action".

Singapore has taken a strong stance on public statements on the Israel-Gaza war, with authorities in the multicultural country insisting this was necessary to preserve racial and social harmony.

The home affairs ministry put out a statement in 2023 advising against "the public display and wearing of articles" in relation to the Israel-Gaza war, including foreign national emblems.

Massive Attack is currently on a world tour, with performances next week in Australia following the end of its Asia leg.

The BBC has contacted the Singaporean police for comment.

News.title: Emma Finucane wins four gold medals in Commonwealth Games first
News.content:
Welsh star Emma Finucane has created history by becoming the first sprint cyclist to win four track gold medals at the same Commonwealth Games.

Finucane added keirin success to the golds she had already won in the team and individual sprints and 1,000m time trial.

Olympic champion Ellesse Andrews finished second when defending her Commonwealth keirin title.

In Birmingham in 2022, New Zealand cyclist Aaron Gate won four gold medals with three on the track and one in the road race.

Finucane has achieved her quartet of successes in four successive days in the Chris Hoy Velodrome in Glasgow.

Australian legend Anna Meares and New Zealander Andrews had previously won three track titles in 2010 and 2022 respectively.

The 23-year-old has also become the first Welsh woman to collect four golds at a single Commonwealth Games.

Finucane is also Wales' most successful female athlete in Games history after overtaking Para-sprinter Olivia Breen, who held the record for two days.

Weightlifter David Morgan remains Wales' most successful Commonwealth Games athlete with nine golds and three silver.

Finucane won Wales' 31st medal of the Games with nine gold, 10 silver and 12 bronze.

The Carmarthen star has also been chosen to be the Team Wales flag bearer for the closing ceremony tonight.

News.title: Three in hospital after fire and crush at festival in London
News.content:
Three people were taken to hospital after a fire and crush at the entrance of a festival.

Organisers of Ghana Party in the Park, also known as Shattafest UK, at Copthall Playing Fields in Barnet, London, said the event was stopped following a "major incident" at about 18:00 BST on Saturday.

The Metropolitan Police said a fire had started near the gates, which meant they were closed temporarily.

A crowd built up, and there was a surge when the gates reopened, it said.

Organisers said the decision to end the festival was made on health and safety grounds.

They said in a statement the day had been "one of the most difficult" in the event's history and called what happened "deeply upsetting".

News.title: Fastest runner to cross the Alps says it was an incredible experience
News.content:
Runner Sophie Woods became the fastest person to complete the 2,000km (1242-mile) Via Alpina ultramarathon beating both the men's and women's record.

Woods ran the route through storms, heat of up to 37C and dodged floods and wildfires across eight countries.

"Through the whole thing, I was only ever thinking about the day, the hour, the sort of minute that I was in", the runner told BBC Breakfast.

The previous record was 35 days and Woods did it in just 29, crediting ice cream slushies for helping her power through.

News.title: Why I don't regret choosing a vasectomy in my 20s
News.content:
Because he was asking for a vasectomy at such a young age, Sam had prepared for the questions his doctor was going to ask him: Don't you think you're too young to know you don't want kids? Could you change your mind in future? You do know reversals are expensive and aren't always successful?

"[The doctor] actually said he had very recently changed his view," says Sam. "And that, if I had come in half a year earlier, he would have turned me away instantly."

His vasectomy took place a couple of months after he first contacted the clinic.

The questions from Sam's doctor were designed to ensure he was making a decision he could live with; men under 30 are more likely to regret a vasectomy, according to guidance from NHS Scotland, external.

Dr Sarah Salkeld, a former GP who is now a medical director for MSI Reproductive Choices, a group of clinics offering various contraceptives to NHS and private patients, says a vasectomy is "very safe and effective".

But she cautions it is important for men to "really think about" whether a vasectomy is right for them.

"We offer everyone counselling to talk about it if they want to, just toâ¦ make sure they've got all the information they need to make that decision."

She says reversals are not routinely available on the NHS as there are strict criteria for having one.

The NHS website points out that other forms of contraception, external are available to men, including condoms and the fertility awareness method - avoiding sex or using condoms on the days when their female partner is most fertile.

Sam told his doctor that, while he loved kids and had a happy childhood himself, he wanted to stay focused on his job as a sound designer for video games.

News.title: Body of mountaineer Nirmal Purja recovered after Pakistan avalanche
News.content:
Prince William said he was "truly saddened to hear of the tragic death" of Purja, who he said "served with distinction" as a soldier before "becoming one of the greatest mountaineers".

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X: "Incredibly sad to learn of the passing of Nirmal (Nims) Purja and those he was climbing with.

"He was an inspirational man who served in our Armed Forces for many years - and whose incredible mountaineering adventures are known the world over."

Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Alpine Club of Pakistan which is involved in the rescue efforts, told BBC's Newshour programme on Saturday that her organisation feared all members of the group were dead, and that Purja had led many expeditions she was on.

Praising his leadership skills, she described him as a "very experienced climber and fearless".

Teams in Pakistan have been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit since Thursday's avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years.

He became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later.

At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity."

Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.

In his last post on X, published on Monday, he said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak.

"Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," Purja wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range.

But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen."

An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level.

"This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence."

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

News.title: Teenager dies after 'medical episode' at Kendal Calling festival in Cumbria
News.content:
A teenage girl died at the Kendal Calling festival in the early hours of the morning, police have said.

The 17-year-old suffered a medical episode at about 02:15 BST and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to Cumbria Police. The force asked people not to speculate about the circumstances of the incident.

It added officers were looking into the circumstances and wanted to speak to anyone who was in the area of the Calling Out tent and the Big Wheel around the time of the girl's death.

A spokesperson said: "Officers are particularly keen to speak with a group of women who alerted first responders to the girl after becoming concerned for her welfare."

They said the girl's family had been informed and were being supported by specialist officers.

The force asked people not to speculate, saying it could have a "significant impact" on the family and friends involved.

"We would ask that the investigation be allowed to take its course."

News.title: Peak District's rebrand deal brings in cash - but also criticism
News.content:
A deal between Peak District bosses and car firm Skoda to put up temporary signs welcoming tourists to "the Peaq District" in honour of the firm's new electric model has given the park authority's coffers a welcome boost.

However, it has also sparked protests from campaigners and residents unhappy about the commercial aspect of the arrangement.

One campaigner said: "If national parks are prepared to sell their very name to the highest bidder, then we're already on the path to industrial extraction of the most protected landscapes."

Park bosses have defended the "fantastic" deal and said the partnership brought in extra funds for conservation and heritage work.

With national parks continuing to grapple with funding pressures, could the partnership be a sign of things to come for the Peak District and beyond?

News.title: Ballot paper for Clacton by-election is longest in British electoral history
News.content:
The longest ballot paper in British political history is costing four times as much to print than regular ballot papers, the local council has said.

The list for the Clacton parliamentary by-election, which was prompted by the resignation of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, is 90cm (3ft) long.

When people unfold the paper, they will find it is longer than most adults' arms.

Tendring District Council chief executive Ian Davidson - who is the acting returning officer for the by-election in the Essex constituency - said organising the vote had been "manic".

People have already started returning postal votes to town hall and most registered voters will go to polling stations on 13 August.

Davidson said: "We've logistically been looking at the size of the ballot paper, how we fold it to get it into the envelope so we can send it out to our postal voters [and] how we manage the polling stations."

News.title: Four arrested over hate crime attack on ship crew
News.content:
Three men have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a Filipino crew member of a cargo ship was attacked in what police described as a hate crime.

Two other men, both also from the Philippines, were also assaulted during the attack involving a large group of people in Avonmouth, near Bristol, on Friday evening.

Police have arrested two men aged 19 and 45, as well as a 17-year-old boy, on suspicion of attempted murder and confirmed they had received reports of racist language being used during the incident.

They remain in custody, as well as a 38-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

News.title: Fires halt trains between London and Stansted Airport
News.content:
Some trains running to and from London Liverpool Street station have been stopped following multiple trackside fires.

At 14:57 BST, Greater Anglia reported a fire at Waltham Cross in Hertfordshire meant all trains had been halted on one line.

The rail operator said London Fire Brigade asked trains to be stopped because of multiple fires close to the railway lines. Smoke is also affecting traffic on the M25, the fire service said.

Rail services to and from Stansted Airport in Essex, Cambridge North, Meridian Water in Hertfordshire and Hertford East are all affected.

News.title: Son of Wicker Man maker dies just weeks before his sequel to film premieres
News.content:
British filmmaker Justin Hardy, who directed a sequel to his late father Robin's 1973 cult horror classic The Wicker Man, has died aged 61.

His family said Hardy died on Friday night after suffering a heart attack, remembering him as "a man of family, of boundless creativity" and "so full of life right to the end".

A Bafta and Emmy nominated writer and director, Hardy was known for the documentary Children of the Wicker Man in 2024, made with his brother Dominic, which chronicled the legacy of their father's iconic film.

He had just completed production on Wrath of the Gods, the concluding chapter to the Wicker Man trilogy, which was due to premiere in London later this month.

Hardy also directed historical films and documentaries for the BBC, Channel 4 and CNN, including Princes In The Tower, Trafalgar Battle Surgeon, The Relief Of Belsen and Spanish Flu: The Forgotten Fallen.

His family said they were "devastated" by his death and "heartbroken" Hardy would not be able to see Wrath of the Gods open.

Dominic described his brother as having "an incredible appetite for life".

"We've lost him and we've lost that larger-than-life presence looking over us all," he said. "He really became a filmmaker his own right."

Dominic also praised Hardy's work on his last film as "incredibly beautiful", adding it was "a great satisfaction to him" to have made something new.

The Wicker Man, starring Edward Woodward and Christopher Lee, is the story of a police officer sent to a remote Scottish island community to investigate the disappearance of a local girl.

Wrath of the Gods was inspired by recently discovered scripts and storyboards by Hardy's late father Robin, marking the end of the trilogy that began with The Wicker Man and the 2011 follow-up The Wicker Tree.

Hardy, who also taught screenwriting at University College London, is survived by his wife Larissa, and their four children.

News.title: Gang of men hurl racist abuse at takeaway owner before violent attack
News.content:
A business owner has said that a group of men hurled racist abuse at him before punching him and smashing his head into a wall in the street in Falkirk.

Dr Zohaib Arshad said the group approached him on Grahams Road last month when he was visiting one of his takeaway shops and asked him when he was "leaving the country" before launching the unprovoked attack.

The 39-year-old, who practised as a vet in Pakistan, patched himself up with glue stitches rather than wait at A&E. He said his children are now fearful of being attacked in school.

BBC Scotland understands the police are treating the incident as a hate crime.

A spokesperson for the force said inquiries into the attack are ongoing.

Arshad stood as an Alba Party candidate for Falkirk at the 2024 General Election and is now a member of the SNP.

His political connections have resulted in the issue being brought to the attention of the Scottish Parliament, external - however he fears it would have gone unnoticed had he been any other member of the public.

News.title: How Emma Finucane mastered the pressure to make Commonwealth Games history
News.content:

Emma Finucane has spent much of the past two years learning how to live with expectation. In Glasgow, she discovered how to thrive under it.

The Welsh cyclist became the first rider in 96 years to complete a Commonwealth Games sprint clean sweep, winning gold in the time trial, sprint, team sprint and keirin.

Yet the significance of the achievement, she revealed, was not just the medals themselves but also the way she dealt with the pressure that came with them.

After winning three medals at Paris 2024, Finucane returned home as one of the most recognisable figures in Olympic sport.

With that status came a new challenge, the knowledge that every rival wanted to beat her.

open image in gallery Emma Finucane had a target on her back as she went for Commonwealth Games history ( Reuters )

“After Paris, I definitely felt like I had a target on my back,” she said. “But I’ve learned to embrace that.

“I’ve learned how to deal with it better and just focus on improving every day.

“After Paris, everything was a huge learning curve for me emotionally too.

“That week was really tough, and what I achieved was difficult to process. But going into these Games, I’ve learned how to handle pressure better and regulate my emotions more.”

That development was evident throughout a week in which Finucane appeared increasingly comfortable with her position as the rider to beat.

In the keirin final, she took the unusual decision to move to the front with two laps remaining, exposing herself to the slipstream of the riders behind her. It was a calculated risk that could have left her vulnerable in the closing stages.

The keirin is cycling’s answer to a chess match played at 70km/h: six riders circling behind a pacing bike before the tactical battle explodes into a final-lap sprint.

But Finucane had already taken control long before the final dash.

She controlled the race from the front and secured the fourth gold medal of a remarkable Games.

open image in gallery Finucane claimed her fourth gold medal of the Games in the keirin ( Reuters )

“I did feel the pressure, of course, especially with people talking about history and what could be achieved,” she said, before a quick shower and change of clothes so she could carry the Welsh flag at the closing ceremony.

“But as an athlete, you don’t really think about that in the moment. You’re just in your own bubble, focused on the next race.

“I knew I had a chance to do something special, but anything can happen in sprinting. I nearly didn’t even get through the semi-final, so it just shows you have to take it one race at a time.“I’m always thinking about the next thing, but I really want to stay in the moment now.

“That’s something I haven’t always been good at, but I’m trying to change that.”

Any suggestion that Finucane’s achievement came against diminished opposition was quickly dismissed by the quality of the riders she defeated.

Olympic champion Ellesse Andrews took silver while defending her title, Katy Marchant – her Olympic team sprint team-mate – finished fifth, while Sophie Capewell, the other member of that Team GB trio, failed to reach the final.

This was no procession.

open image in gallery Finucane had to beat off stern competition to top the podium ( Reuters )

Finucane’s achievement also secured her a place in Welsh sporting history. She became the first Welsh woman to win four gold medals at a single Commonwealth Games, moving beyond para-sprinter Olivia Breen’s record as Wales’ most successful female athlete at the event.

The overall Welsh record remains with weightlifter David Morgan, whose haul of nine gold medals and three silver medals makes him the nation’s most decorated Commonwealth athlete.

“I just hope I’ve inspired people back home to get on a bike or into a velodrome,” she added.

“I’m so glad I found this sport – or maybe it found me. I absolutely love what I do.”

Away from the track, Finucane’s week also contained distracting questions about her partner Matt Richardson, who was forced to withdraw from the Commonwealth Games after suffering an injury.

Richardson, who controversially switched allegiance from Australia to Great Britain, had been expected to compete in Glasgow but was ruled out before the start of the competition.

open image in gallery Finucane said the support of Matt Richardson was crucial throughout her historic week ( Getty )

Despite his absence, Finucane said his support — alongside that of her family — had been crucial throughout her historic week.

“My mum, dad, sister and her partner were all here, and my brother was watching from home,” she said. “My partner was even on FaceTime from Japan at 2am. That support network is everything to me.”

“My partner was even on FaceTime from Japan at 2am. That support network is everything to me. They love me no matter what, win or lose, and that takes all the pressure away.”

For now, though, Finucane is determined not to look too far ahead. First comes a holiday to Corfu before she narrows her focus on October's World Championships and then the 2028 Olympics.

“I just want to keep riding my bike, keep enjoying it, and keep improving," she added.

"I’m grateful for everything I’ve achieved, and I don’t take any of it for granted.”

Wildfires continue to devastate eastern Washington state, forcing the evacuation of approximately 5,000 homes and destroying around 600 residential and commercial properties, authorities reported.

The blazes, which remain uncontained, have scorched more than 8 square miles around Spokane, Washington's second-largest city, and are among dozens stretching emergency resources across the western U.S.

No fatalities have been reported in the Spokane area.

The situation in Spokane is particularly challenging due to adverse weather and terrain.

Benjamin Cossel, public information officer for a federal response team deployed from California, noted, "We have weather working against us, and we have terrain working against us."

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

Wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph were anticipated, exacerbating the spread of the Old Trails, Fairview, and Meadowview Fires.

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a state of emergency, and the National Weather Service issued a "particularly dangerous situation" red flag alert for eastern Washington.

Cossel explained that the Spokane River, which bisects the city of 229,000, is flanked by steep canyons that funnel winds.

As temperatures rise, cooler air near the ground ascends, allowing these powerful winds to sweep through the area.

"They push the fire through the canyons, up, up the slopes, and then outside the slopes and around," he said, describing the "turbulent, really challenging sort of wind scenarios" created by the hilly and steep landscape.

open image in gallery ( Reuters )

Meanwhile, a massive wildfire in western Idaho and eastern Oregon has been burning for 10 days, consuming nearly 525 square miles of grassland. This blaze, which authorities attribute to lightning, threatens over 600 homes and 800 other structures in an area vital for cattle ranching.

The regional weather forecast offers little relief, with sunny and dry conditions expected to persist well into the week. Temperatures are projected to climb above 90 degrees Fahrenheit by Wednesday.

The National Weather Service has issued air quality warnings for eastern Washington, eastern Oregon, western and central Idaho, and western Montana. Red flag fire warnings are in effect for parts of Utah, Montana, and western Nebraska, alongside extreme heat warnings for southern Arizona, California, Nevada, and northern Montana.

In Spokane, authorities have established a shelter at the city's main convention center for displaced residents. Keila Vizcarra, spokesperson for the federal team managing the "Big Grass Fire" in Idaho and Oregon, underscored the widespread impact, stating, "The whole northwest is heavily impacted right now."

Democratic Rep. Ted Lieu, a member of the House Judiciary Committee, promised to investigate the government’s botched attempt to charge a former Olympian with damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool liner.

Sunday morning, Lieu accused U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro of trying to “destroy the life” of David Hearn by charging him with felony destruction of property “based on false evidence.”

“This is radical, unethical and unconscionable behavior,” Lieu wrote on X. “Democrats will investigate. November is coming.”

His assertion came two days after Pirro motioned to drop the charges against Hearn, admitting in a court filing that the damage to the pool liner was the result of poor installation.

Pirro’s reversal came as a surprise, given she, President Donald Trump and other members of the administration have been categorical that the damage was the result of “vandals” who were motivated by ideological differences.

open image in gallery Democrats condemned US Attorney Jeanine Pirro’s office for bringing charges against a former Olympian, seemingly without having all the facts first ( Reuters )

Even Trump appeared shocked, writing on Truth Social, “I don’t know what she was thinking?” The president insisted vandals were responsible for the damage.

But Pirro’s filing claims that the Interior Department had misled her office into bringing the charges without the full scope of evidence. However, with new documentation on the table, Pirro said the materials “significantly undermine the evidentiary basis for the indictment.”

The change has led lawmakers from both sides of the aisle to raise their eyebrows at how such an indictment could have been brought without all the information necessary.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, called Pirro’s charges “bogus,” and wrote on X that “every failed prosecution [is] a self-indictment.”

open image in gallery David Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist, had pleaded not guilty to destruction of property charges – which the government now requests to be dismissed ( Reuters )

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, wrote on X Saturday that Hearn should be able to seek remedy for the “maliciously prosecuted” case.

Blumenthal pushed for legislation, co-sponsored by Senator Alex Padilla, that would hold prosecutors accountable.

Republican Senator John Kennedy told NBC’s Meet the Press Sunday that “the whole thing is a multiple-vehicle pile-up.”

“I don't know why she filed a suit without doing a full investigation,” Kennedy said, adding that “if she can’t prove her case she was right to pull back. Because if you fool around with a federal judge, you will find out.”

open image in gallery President Trump has continued to insist that vandals are responsible for damaging the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, despite a recent court filing indicating it was the result of poor installation ( AFP/Getty )

Kennedy went on to cast doubt over Trump’s assertion that vandals damaged the Reflecting Pool.

“I don’t know whether he really believes that or it’s part of his political messaging or he’s just thinking out loud. He exists loudly, and he grows anxious when he has an unexpressed thought. I’m not saying he doesn’t really believe it, I just don’t know,” Kennedy said.

Republican Rep. Jim Jordan told CNN’s State of the Union Sunday that, while he wasn’t clear on the facts, he would be bothered if Pirro’s office was trying to send an innocent man to jail.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Sunday that FIFA President Gianni Infantino was not the right man to lead world soccer’s governing body in the latest fallout from the now abandoned plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

“I do not believe that he is the right man to lead football forward on the world stage," Burnham said. “The plan that was put forward was offensive to many people, football people, around the world, and it can’t be the case that we just move on and forget that, it wasn’t acceptable."

On Saturday, European soccer's governing body UEFA said it had lost confidence in FIFA’s leadership — possibly paving the way for a challenge to Infantino’s presidency. The governing body for North and Central American and Caribbean soccer (CONCACAF) said FIFA leadership had “stopped putting football first.”

Infantino was forced into a backdown over his controversial plans to sell World Cup profits through a commercial subsidiary that would run its top competitions.

Infantino’s plans fell apart after UEFA’s 55-member nations agreed Thursday to boycott the World Cup and all other FIFA competitions. CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation also said they opposed the plan.

Despite Infantino's climbdown, UEFA said it would work with other confederations to "devise a plan to make sure that it cannot occur again.”

“No option should be off the table,” it said.

While Infantino has received pockets of public support from associations including 2022 World Cup host Qatar, Burnham's words were further evidence of the anger generated by his plans.

The next FIFA presidential election is in March in Rabat, Morocco. The deadline for candidates to enter the presidential contest is Nov. 18, exactly four months ahead of the vote.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, a Republican from Ohio, broke his silence around the horrific abuse claims his daughter has leveled against her ex-husband Rep. Max Miller on Sunday, calling for Miller to resign and seek mental health treatment.

Moreno issued a statement on Sunday only minutes after Miller himself read a statement on a live stream denying claims of abuse against his ex-wife and two-year-old daughter.

“As he has admitted privately, Max Miller needs serious psychological help. He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter,” read the senator’s statement in part. “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives.”

He added: “It has been horrific to watch this play out in full public view, all while knowing an innocent two-year-old girl is caught in the middle. Our priority has always been protecting our daughter and our granddaughter. Out of concern for the safety of my family, I hoped to keep this matter private but Max Miller’s increasingly erratic and dangerous behavior has made that impossible.”

The embattled congressman is suing his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, and her attorney over claims they’ve made that Miller allegedly held a gun to Emily’s head, broke his daughter’s collarbone, and engaged in drug use, as well as assaulted her by pouring hot or scalding water on her, all of which he denies.

open image in gallery Rep. Max Miller is suing his ex-wife for defamation while he himself faces a similar case brought by an ex-girlfriend and former Trump White House aide ( Getty )

He is separately facing a lawsuit from ex-Trump White House aide Stephanie Grisham, who dated him in 2019 and 2020 and was sued by him after she accused him, without naming him directly, of domestic abuse in a Washington Post op-ed. Grisham claims he violated the terms of a nondisclosure agreement they signed to settle that lawsuit, by claiming she was lying.

“Defendants engaged in a defamatory campaign against Plaintiff to malign his character, undermine his odds at re-election to Congress and falsely portray him as a violent and abusive father and husband,” his attorneys wrote in a court filing.

Miller appeared on video to deny all allegations he faces.

"No court or agency has even substantiated any allegation against me," said the congressman. "Every single one of these allegations were already investigated."

"I'm not getting out of this race, and I'm winning in November," he continued.

Miller did not address the senator, a fellow Republican, during his own livestream. He later did so on X, writing to Moreno: “@berniemoreno If my daughter said the same thing to me, I personally wouldn’t wait two years before holding him accountable. You know this isn’t true and the only reason you are speaking out now is to hide from your own media circus. This is all political.”

Rep. Mike Turner, Miller’s colleague in the House, was asked about the situation on CBS’s Face the Nation on Sunday. Turner dodged questions about whether Republican leadership or voters should take up the issue before November, when Miller is up for re-election, and instead repeated that the allegations should be handled in “court” and not “a television studio”. He also would not answer whether the House Ethics Committee should take up an investigation into Miller’s alleged behavior.

open image in gallery Sen. Bernie Moreno called for his former son-in-law to resign from Congress on Sunday ( Getty )

open image in gallery House leadership under Mike Johnson is facing increased pressure to address the Miller allegations ( Reuters )

Republicans, including Sen. Moreno before his statement Sunday, have been facing increasing pressure to address the allegations leveled at Miller by his ex-wife and ex-girlfriend for days. The district Miller represents is a safe Republican seat but still has some on the right worried about the damage the explosive nature of the allegations could do, both as it relates to his re-election chances and those of other Republicans.

An ugly intra-party spat is the last thing Republicans need in Ohio as the state is home to a crucial Senate race this cycle and the congressional GOP caucuses are trying to protect thin dual majorities under the cloud of Donald Trump’s sinking approval ratings and dissatisfaction with Washington’s lack of focus on affordability.

A spokesperson for Emily Moreno also released a statement, responding to Miller’s livestream appearance.

“It is shameful that Max Miller decided to go on a bizarre and lie-filled rant about his ex-wife to desperately try to save his political career. There is a documented trove of evidence that Miller has a history of violent and dangerous behavior and no amount of victim shaming will change that,” said Stefan Mychajliw.

“It is despicable and abhorrent that Miller lied on an unhinged and humiliating video for their daughter to watch one day. No loving parent would have ever used their daughter as a PR pawn to save their own political career. Miller can lie and spin on X, but he cannot do so under oath in a court of law. We are confident that justice will prevail in court.”

Rumors of allegations leveled against Miller were a open secret within the GOP caucus and were openly referenced by Rep. George Santos on the House floor in 2023 during a spat with the congressman before the latter’s conviction and imprisonment on fraud charges. Miller, at the time, led an effort among Republicans to expel Santos from the House.
