World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018835/Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.title: Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018835/Shaw in Shanghai: How the Irish Writer’s 1933 Visit Inspired China’s Literati
World.content:
Editor’s note: The theme of the third Shanghai Public Relations Academic Symposium on Irish Literature, held on July 26, was playwright George Bernard Shaw’s eight-hour visit to Shanghai in the 1930s, when China’s cultural and anti-imperialist movements were gaining momentum. The following is an account of the writer’s time in the city and its impact on Chinese intellectuals.

When George Bernard Shaw, the Irish playwright and novelist, paid a brief visit to Shanghai as part of his global voyage in 1933, the city’s intellectuals were thrilled.

Before his arrival, articles about Shaw had been published in various newspapers and magazines. Some discussed his Communist advocacy in Hong Kong, while others talked about how his satirical writing style had influenced European society.

According to a biography of Soong Ching Ling, the Chinese politician and wife of Sun Yat-sen, sometimes called the “father of modern China,” Shaw arrived at Wusongkou port — today the Wusongkou International Cruise Terminal in northeastern Shanghai — at 6 a.m. on Feb. 17 aboard the Empress of Britain, accompanied by his wife, the political activist Charlotte Payne-Townshend. At 5 a.m., Soong went to Wusongkou with Yang Xingfo, a social activist and patriotic democrat, to welcome the couple. At Shaw’s invitation, she joined him on board for breakfast.

More than 200 reporters rushed to Wusongkou early that morning, but Shaw initially refused to go ashore, telling Soong that apart from her, there was no one in Shanghai he wanted to meet, nor anything he wanted to see. But in the end, Soong persuaded him to pay a visit to the city. They took a steamship to Lanlu Wharf in today’s Yangpu District, where he finally went ashore. The reporters waiting at Wusongkou left empty-handed — not a single photograph of Shaw was taken.

At 10:30 a.m., Soong and Shaw disembarked and set out for the city’s downtown. Shaw met and talked with several left-wing Chinese intellectuals, including Yang, former Peking University president Cai Yuanpei, literary icon Lu Xun, writer and linguist Lin Yutang, and the American journalists Harold Isaacs and Agnes Smedley.

Later, at the invitation of the Chinese branch of PEN International, a global association of writers founded in London in 1921, Shaw and other Chinese intellectuals visited the World College on Route Ferguson (now Wukang Road) to attend a gathering with local PEN members. When Shaw met Mei Lanfang, the renowned Peking opera artist and founder of Shanghai’s Left Theatre Club, he expressed his puzzlement over the differences between Eastern and Western theater.

“Will you please tell me how a Chinese actor can do anything in the midst of such infernal uproars as one hears on your stage?” he asked. “In our theater, they put a man out if he sneezes. But you have gongs and cymbals and the competition of half the audience and innumerable vendors. Don’t you object?”

Mei explained that Peking opera was a folk art first performed in the open air, and drums and gongs were then used to attract people to the show. This tradition had simply endured.

Around 3 p.m., Shaw finally spoke with some Chinese and foreign reporters in the garden of Soong’s residence, discussing socialism, national oppression, Eastern culture, and revolutions, among other topics. Afterward, Soong accompanied Shaw back to the Empress of Britain, which then carried the playwright northward to Beijing.

Although Shaw spent just over eight hours in Shanghai, his visit sparked considerable discussion and reverberations among the city’s left-wing intellectual circles. The writer and poet Yu Dafu wrote in Free Talk, a supplement of the Shun Pao newspaper, that he hoped Shaw could tell the world, in his own sarcastic tone, about Japanese imperialism and its invasion of China.

At the time, intellectuals including Lu Xun and the poet and translator Qu Qiubai were working to build a central stronghold for China’s left-wing cultural movement. After Shaw’s departure, they, along with partners Xu Guangping and Yang Zhihua, began compiling reports from various newspapers and periodicals about the Irish novelist’s short visit. The collection was published in March 1933 by Yecao Shudian, or Wildgrass Bookshop, under the title “George Bernard Shaw in Shanghai.”

In the preface, Lu wrote: “Those who truly welcomed him were the Chinese people, as well as the literary and artistic circles that stood by the people. The Chinese people did not regard him as a ‘revolutionary leader’ or a ‘thoroughgoing socialist writer,’ much less as an idol. They regarded Shaw as a loyal friend of the oppressed people of the world, and of China.”

Editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from the Shanghai Lu Xun Museum, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.title: How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018830/How Cantonese Cuisine Became Part of the English Language
World.content:
This is the first article in a two-part series exploring how Chinese culinary terms came to be included in the Oxford English Dictionary (OED).

For more than two decades, I have studied how Chinese words enter the English language, particularly through food. So when the Oxford English Dictionary (OED) released its second batch of updates this past June, one updated entry felt especially meaningful to me: “Cantonese.” For the first time, the dictionary formally recognized the word as a culinary term, defining it as food prepared in the style of Guangzhou and the surrounding region in southern China, as well as the restaurants that serve such cuisine.

The entry is accompanied not just by a simple definition, but by a timeline of citations tracing the term’s culinary history. The earliest example dates back to April 6, 1892, when New Jersey’s Trenton Times referred to “Fashionable Cantonese dishes.” This phrase shows that the term was already being used in relation to food more than a century ago, long before the era of modern globalization.

Western interest in Cantonese cuisine also stretches back to the late 19th century. The OED cites an 1894 report from The Washington Post describing a dim sum dumpling as “shaped exactly like a fishing creel.” By 1908, The New York Herald was explaining the dish to its readers by comparing it to a “second cousin to steamed sponge cake.” These early descriptions reveal how unfamiliar foods were introduced to Western audiences through comparisons with things they already understood.

Over the following decades, Cantonese cuisine continued to leave its mark. A 1950 publication by the Hong Kong Young Women’s Christian Association highlighted “Cantonese specialties” such as turnip pudding, while a 1997 culinary memoir recalled dining at a large “Cantonese restaurant” where dim sum was served from rolling trolleys. More recently, a 2015 article in The Guardian recommended Wong Chi Kee in Hong Kong for its “traditional Cantonese congee.”

These citations connect to a broader ecosystem of existing terms. The Cantonese practice of yum cha, literally “drinking tea,” the social meal of dim sum and tea traditionally enjoyed in the morning, was added to the dictionary in 2016, while dim sum has appeared in the dictionary since 1989.

Today, my research shows that the dictionary contains a vocabulary of 25 Cantonese culinary terms. Beyond the widely recognized dim sum and yum cha, the list includes char siu, wonton, chop suey, hoisin sauce, egg foo yung, and moo goo gai pan. These are no longer treated as foreign concepts requiring lengthy explanations; they have become established English words.

Yet this lexicographical milestone is not simply a retrospective look at history; it also reflects a living culture. Just months earlier, in March 2026, three new additions expanded the OED’s Cantonese culinary vocabulary: dan tat (egg tart), pineapple bun, and yin yeung (a Hong Kong drink combining milk tea and coffee). Their inclusion highlights that Cantonese cuisine is not a static relic of the past. It continues to evolve, innovate, and influence the English language. This ongoing linguistic exchange shows that the relationship between East and West remains an active and continuing process.

The contrast with other regional Chinese cuisines highlights that global influence is not simply a product of modern international presence. Shanghai, for instance, is one of China’s most globally connected cities, yet its local Benbang cuisine has left far fewer traces in the English language. Cantonese cuisine’s deep roots in English developed instead through generations of migration, trade, and everyday use.

Etymologically, “Cantonese” derives from “Canton,” the former English name for Guangzhou, which was first recorded by Portuguese traders in the 16th century. Over time, the term evolved from a geographic reference into a marker of a distinct cultural and culinary identity. This reflects a broader historical reality: Cantonese cuisine established an overseas presence earlier than many other regional Chinese cuisines, spreading through centuries of maritime trade and migration.

Historically, because the vast majority of early Chinese immigrants to many Western countries came from Guangdong, Cantonese restaurants dominated many Chinatowns. Iconic establishments such as New York’s Port Arthur Restaurant, which opened in 1897 and introduced upscale Cantonese dishes to Western diners, and San Francisco’s Shanghai Low, a Cantonese restaurant that adopted a Shanghai-inspired name to appeal to Western customers, did more than serve food. They became gathering places for immigrant communities and helped establish Cantonese cuisine’s prominence in Western societies.

As a linguist, I often argue that translation is not merely a tool for communication between languages; it is also a means of cultural understanding. The inclusion of these terms shows that English speakers are capable of adopting culinary vocabulary from other languages on its own terms.

For readers interested in exploring this vocabulary, here are eight popular Cantonese culinary terms currently included in the OED, with condensed definitions for clarity.

Many of the early Cantonese restaurants that introduced these dishes to Western audiences have since disappeared. Yet the vocabulary they helped popularize has endured, and a new generation of Cantonese restaurants continues to thrive in Chinatowns and communities around the world. The OED’s recognition of Cantonese cuisine reflects this longer history of cultural exchange: carried across borders by generations of immigrants, Cantonese food has become a lasting part of the global culinary vocabulary.

(Header and in-text images: Visuals from VCG, edited by Ding Yining/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.title: China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018828/China’s Largest Bookstore Launches Nationwide Same-Day Delivery
World.content:
Chinese state-owned bookstore chain Xinhua Bookstore is partnering with food delivery giant Meituan to roll out a nationwide same-day book delivery service, promising to deliver books in under an hour.

The agreement, signed on Friday at the 34th National Book Expo in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, will connect the more than 10,000 Xinhua stores across China to Meituan’s instant retail network, Instashopping. Customers ordering through the network will be able to receive books in as quickly as 30 minutes.

The initiative marks the expansion of multiple pilot initiatives in the last two years comprising several regional Xinhua branches, including in Zhejiang, Shanghai, and the southern city of Shenzhen.

Founded in 1937, Xinhua is China’s largest and oldest bookstore chain.

Instant retail combines online ordering with inventories from nearby physical stores and a network of couriers to deliver products rapidly, typically in under one hour. China’s instant retail market is expected to surpass 1 trillion yuan ($150 billion) in 2026 and double to 2 trillion yuan by 2030, according to a report by the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation.

The push into instant retail comes amid intensifying competition between China’s e-commerce platforms and weakening demand for printed books. The country’s book retail market totaled roughly 110 billion yuan in 2025, down 2% from 2024, according to a report by Chinese analytics firm OpenBook.

Jiang Chuanyang, chairman of Xinhua’s Zhejiang branch, said at the event that China’s book market is evolving to comprise e-commerce, local instant retail, and physical bookstores. More than 100 stores in the province were active on Instashopping throughout 2025, generating combined sales of several million yuan, according to domestic media.

But the picture is more mixed for independent bookstores.

Su Shanna, brand manager of Yinxu, a chain of five bookstores in the eastern coastal city of Xiamen, told Sixth Tone that instant delivery orders account for roughly 15% of the company’s monthly revenue. The store joined Instashopping in May 2025, and also accepts on-demand orders through its WeChat mini program, fulfilling local deliveries through courier services such as SF Express and JD Logistics.

“It’s more of a bonus than a lifeline,” Su said, noting that demand for instant book delivery remains limited to a handful of scenarios. These include parents ordering extracurricular reading materials or textbooks for their children, tourists ordering books to their hotels, and patients looking for something to read during hospitalization.

Instant retail fills the gap where consumers need a book immediately and traditional e-commerce can’t meet the demand, according to Jiang Han, a senior researcher at Beijing-based think tank Pangoal.

But books are a low-profit business. Because instant retail platforms take a cut of bookstore sales, instant delivery is unlikely to become a major profit driver, he said.

The service’s real value isn’t in generating significant new revenue, but in generating new revenue sources, Jiang added. “Its significance should be on how it helps bookstores reconstruct their connection to readers.”

Jiang said that bookstores are increasingly trying to become “cultural service hubs” by diversifying their revenue sources, selling tourism-related products, and integrating with the local community. Instant retail is part of this trend.

In the case of Yinxu, members pay an annual fee of 188 yuan, which gives them discounts on books, book delivery services, and tickets to local performances, as well as access to various community activities.

“The key to success depends on whether bookstores can offer irreplaceable cultural experiences and emotional value,” Jiang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from iNueng/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.title: China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018827/China’s Short-Drama Boom Calls for a New AI Crew
World.content:
One graduate trained to restore ancient artifacts now generates AI video clips for short dramas. Another, schooled in landscape design, builds virtual scenery instead of physical sets.

Both are part of a hiring surge across China’s film industry, as AI creates demand for hybrid creative roles and cuts production timelines from months to days. Recruitment for AI video editors jumped 179% year over year in June, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

At one cultural communications company in Zhengzhou, capital of China’s central Henan province, monthly production of AI-generated short dramas has risen from a handful to nearly 100, according to CCTV. The expansion has created demand for AI video editors and “card pullers,” who write prompts, generate footage, and select clips that fit a production’s characters and plot.

The shift is drawing workers from fields including design, animation, digital media, and information technology, according to recruitment platform Zhaopin. AI film roles typically pay between 8,000 and 20,000 yuan ($1,100 to $2,800) a month, depending on experience.

“This indicates that AI is not simply a substitution, but a technological enabler that is driving the transformation of traditional professions and roles,” Li Qiang, a vice president at Zhaopin, told CCTV.

AI is also changing how short dramas are made. Some productions that once required crews of dozens can now be completed by a few people, or even one creator handling scripts, storyboards, visuals, and effects. CCTV reported that AI has compressed some production cycles from months to days, with certain episodes completed in hours and effects and previsualization work becoming three to 10 times faster.

Director He Ziqiang, an early adopter of AI filmmaking tools, has added AI storyboard artists, image generators, card pullers, and editors to his team, many without formal film training.

“Anyone can make their own film, as long as they have ideas,” He told CCTV. “This will greatly enrich artistic creation and vitality, enabling more talented ordinary people to express themselves through AI.”

The hiring surge comes as China’s short-drama industry’s annual output value approached 90 billion yuan in 2025, nearly double the previous year, while some AI-generated productions have reported net profit margins above 50%.

Li Yuan, who is not related to Li Qiang, founder of a Henan-based AI film company, told domestic media his firm had cut the cost of producing a drama from 300,000 yuan to 50,000 yuan while increasing output.

“We thought large models would take longer to nail video fluency, but they got it done in the first quarter of this year,” Li told state media.

But he also cautioned that AI short dramas remain at an early stage, with both the technology and audience tastes still evolving. “Only when the market stabilizes can creators and platforms offer better products,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Staff at a short-drama production company use AI tools during post-production in Jiaxing, Zhejiang province, July 21, 2026. VCG)

World.title: Landfall possible for Tropical Depression Luis, but track ‘highly uncertain’
World.content:
PAGASA says Tropical Depression Luis could make landfall in Northern Luzon on Monday afternoon or evening, August 3

MANILA, Philippines – The weather bureau is now seeing possible landfall for Tropical Depression Luis in Northern Luzon, but it noted that Luis’ track is “highly uncertain” and may still change.

As of 10 pm on Sunday, August 2, Luis was already 200 kilometers east of Baler, Aurora, moving west northwest at 15 kilometers per hour (km/h).

The tropical depression maintained its strength, with maximum sustained winds of 55 km/h and gustiness of up to 70 km/h.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said in its 11 pm bulletin on Sunday that Luis could make landfall in Northern Luzon on Monday afternoon or evening, August 3.

“Afterwards, it will slowly turn northeastward then east northeastward while moving away from the Philippine landmass,” added PAGASA.

Luis is also projected to intensify into a tropical storm by Monday morning, but it could weaken back into a tropical depression after several hours. Eventually, it may be downgraded to a remnant low by Wednesday, August 5.

Luis continues to affect nearly the entire Luzon. Within the next 48 hours, it is now expected to bring up to intense rain, particularly in the provinces of Zambales and Pangasinan, while at least 18 other areas may get heavy rain from the tropical depression. Floods and landslides could occur.

Sunday evening, August 2, to Monday evening, August 3

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): La Union, Pangasinan, Benguet, Cagayan, Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino, Zambales, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Aurora, Quezon

Monday evening, August 3, to Tuesday evening, August 4

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Zambales, Pangasinan

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Sur, La Union, Benguet, Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino, Aurora, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bataan, Metro Manila, Cavite, Batangas, Rizal

Elsewhere in Luzon, scattered rain and thunderstorms may persist because of Luis.

PAGASA also warned the public that the southwest monsoon or habagat will be dumping rain, mainly in Luzon too:

Monday evening, August 3, to Tuesday evening, August 4

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Occidental Mindoro

Tuesday evening, August 4, to Wednesday evening, August 5

Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Zambales, Bataan, Occidental Mindoro

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): La Union, Pangasinan, Benguet, Nueva Ecija, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, Antique

The southwest monsoon will be enhanced by the tropical cyclone with the international name Dolphin, which is currently a typhoon outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

Meanwhile, Signal No. 1 was lifted for portions of Bicol at 11 pm on Sunday, but new places in Northern Luzon and Central Luzon were added to the list. These areas will have strong winds due to Luis:

southern part of Cagayan (Enrile, Tuguegarao City, Peñablanca)

Isabela

Quirino

northern part of Aurora (Dinalungan, Casiguran, Dilasag, Dipaculao, Baler)

Polillo Islands

northern part of Camarines Norte (Daet, Talisay, Paracale, Jose Panganiban, Capalonga, Vinzons)

PAGASA is not ruling out the possibility of raising Signal No. 2 if Luis becomes a tropical storm.

The southwest monsoon and Luis’ periphery or outer bands are also bringing strong to gale-force gusts to these areas:

Monday, August 3, and Tuesday, August 4

most of Luzon, most of Visayas, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Camiguin, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Sarangani, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

On Monday, moderate to rough conditions are expected in the following seaboards:

Eastern seaboards of Isabela and Davao Oriental; northeastern seaboard of Aurora – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Eastern seaboards of Batanes, Cagayan, Dinagat Islands, Surigao del Sur, and Davao Occidental; northern and eastern seaboards of Polillo Islands, Catanduanes, and Northern Samar; northern seaboards of Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, and Masbate; southern seaboard of Davao Oriental; western seaboard of Bataan – waves up to 2 meters high

Small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible.

After weakening into a remnant low by Wednesday, Luis could become “fully assimilated” or absorbed into Dolphin’s circulation.

The typhoon was located 3,000 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon as of 8 pm on Sunday, still moving west northwest at 25 km/h. Its maximum sustained winds decreased from 175 km/h to 165 km/h, while its gustiness eased from 215 km/h to 205 km/h.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Grace Castañeda-Carpio earlier said Dolphin appears “less likely” to enter PAR, but the weather bureau is not ruling out this possibility. What is more certain is that Dolphin will enhance the southwest monsoon.

Luis is the Philippines’ 12th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for August. PAGASA earlier said two to four tropical cyclones could develop within or enter PAR during the month. – Rappler.com

World.title: Romeo Jalosjos, former Zamboanga del Norte congressman, dies at 85
World.content:
The wake and viewing services will be held at The Heritage Park in Taguig City from August 3 to 5, and will then be moved to the family-owned Gloria de Dapitan Complex in Dapitan City from August 6 to August 12.

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – Former Zamboanga del Norte 1st District congressman Romeo Jalosjos has died, his son Seth announced on Sunday, August 2. He was 85.

Jalosjos was a member of the Ferdinand E. Marcos-era Batasang Pambansa. He later returned to Congress as representative of Zamboanga del Norte in the 1990s.

His political career was marred by controversy after he was accused of raping an 11-year-old girl, a charge he denied. The Supreme Court in 2002 upheld his conviction for statutory rape, ending his tenure in the House of Representatives and barring him from continuing in public office.

His prison sentence was later commuted by then-president Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, and he was released in 2009.

Despite his conviction and removal from office, Jalosjos remained a major political figure in Zamboanga del Norte. He was the patriarch of one of the province’s most influential political families, with several of his children and relatives later holding elected positions in local and national government.

ALSO ON RAPPLER

Beyond politics, Jalosjos was a wealthy businessman. He was among those who started the noontime television show Eat Bulaga!

He was also behind Dakak, a well-known luxury beach resort in Dapitan City.

His son Seth said the wake and viewing services will be held at The Heritage Park in Taguig City from August 3 to 5, and will then be moved to the family-owned Gloria de Dapitan Complex in Dapitan City from August 6 to August 12.

In a statement, the Jalosjos family said he dedicated his life to public service and community development. They described him as “a leader who listened, a champion of the underserved, and a father to his people.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Tropical Depression Luis bringing heavy rain to more areas
World.content:
Even as it stays offshore, Tropical Depression Luis is affecting nearly the entire Luzon, says PAGASA on Sunday afternoon, August 2

MANILA, Philippines – The weather bureau on Sunday afternoon, August 2, warned more areas to brace for significant rainfall from Tropical Depression Luis in the next couple of days.

Luis was last spotted 285 kilometers east of Baler, Aurora, at 4 pm on Sunday. The tropical depression continues to move northwest at 15 kilometers per hour, with maximum sustained winds of 55 km/h and gustiness of up to 70 km/h.

In a briefing past 5 pm on Sunday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said Luis is still likely to stay over the Philippine Sea. But it could go near or make landfall in Northern Luzon or Central Luzon if its track shifts westward.

Luis might also strengthen into a tropical storm in a matter of hours, but it may weaken back into a tropical depression by Tuesday, August 4, and into a remnant low by Wednesday, August 5.

Based on PAGASA’s updated rainfall advisory issued at 5 pm on Sunday, the following areas may be the most affected by Luis in the next 48 hours:

Sunday afternoon, August 2, to Monday afternoon, August 3

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Pangasinan, Cagayan, Isabela, Quirino, Zambales, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Aurora, Quezon

Monday afternoon, August 3, to Tuesday afternoon, August 4

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): La Union, Pangasinan, Benguet, Isabela, Quirino, Aurora, Nueva Ecija, Bulacan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Zambales, Bataan, Metro Manila, Cavite, Batangas, Rizal

Aside from the areas mentioned above, Luis is also affecting the rest of the Ilocos Region, the rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of Central Luzon, the rest of Calabarzon, Metro Manila, Bicol, the Cordillera Administrative Region, Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Marinduque, Romblon, and Western Visayas on Sunday evening. Scattered rain and thunderstorms are expected to persist.

Aside from Luis, the southwest monsoon or habagat will be another major source of rain in the coming week, as it will be enhanced by the tropical cyclone with the international name Dolphin, which is currently a typhoon outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR). Here is the latest rainfall outlook for the southwest monsoon:

Tuesday afternoon, August 4, to Wednesday afternoon, August 5

Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): La Union, Pangasinan, Benguet, Tarlac, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Cavite, Rizal, Batangas, Antique

Meanwhile, fewer areas are under Signal No. 1 due to Luis as of 5 pm on Sunday, as its strong winds are likely to remain mostly offshore:

Polillo Islands

Camarines Norte

northern part of Camarines Sur (Caramoan, Garchitorena, Lagonoy, Tinambac, Siruma)

northern part of Catanduanes (Pandan, Caramoran, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga)

PAGASA is not ruling out the possibility of raising Signal No. 2 if Luis becomes a tropical storm.

The southwest monsoon and Luis’ periphery or outer bands are also bringing strong to gale-force gusts to these areas:

Sunday, August 2

Marinduque, Occidental Mindoro, Oriental Mindoro, Romblon, Masbate, Sorsogon, Caluya Islands, Northern Samar, Samar, Biliran, Siquijor, Southern Leyte, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands

Monday, August 3, and Tuesday, August 4

most of Luzon, most of Visayas, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Camiguin, Surigao del Norte, Dinagat Islands, Sarangani, Davao Occidental, Davao Oriental

In the next 24 hours, moderate to rough conditions are likely in the following seaboards:

Eastern seaboard of Davao Oriental – waves up to 2.5 meters high

Seaboards of Isabela, Surigao del Sur, and Davao Occidental; eastern seaboards of Cagayan, Catanduanes, and Northern Samar; northern seaboards of Aurora, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, and Catanduanes; remaining seaboard of Davao Oriental – waves up to 2 meters high

Small vessels should take precautionary measures or avoid sailing, if possible.

After weakening into a remnant low by Wednesday, Luis could become “fully assimilated” or absorbed into Dolphin’s circulation.

The typhoon was located 3,100 kilometers east of extreme Northern Luzon as of 4 pm on Sunday, still moving west northwest at 25 km/h. It still has maximum sustained winds of 175 km/h and gustiness of up to 215 km/h.

PAGASA Weather Specialist Grace Castañeda-Carpio said Dolphin appears “less likely” to enter PAR, but the weather bureau is not ruling out this possibility. What is more certain is that Dolphin will enhance the southwest monsoon.

Luis is the Philippines’ 12th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for August. PAGASA earlier said two to four tropical cyclones could develop within or enter PAR during the month. – Rappler.com

World.title: Jobert Sucaldito, veteran PH entertainment figure, dies at 65
World.content:
HOST. Jobert Sucaldito anchored his own radio program on DZMM.

One of the most recognizable names in Philippine entertainment media, Jobert Sucaldito worked across various platforms, including television, radio, and print

MANILA, Philippines – Veteran entertainment personality Jobert Sucaldito died on Sunday, August 2. He was 65.

Sucaldito’s death was confirmed by Chaps Manansala, his partner on the online show Oras ng Opinyon Talakayan at Diskusyon (OOTD).

“Thank you very much for your unwavering love, support, prayers, and continued support for him throughout the years. His memories, kindness, and the stories that he left behind will remain alive in our hearts,” read a statement posted in Filipino by the OOTD Jobert and Chaps Channel on its Facebook page.

“We ask for your prayers for his eternal rest and for our family during this time of deep grief.”

According to the OOTD Jobert and Chaps Channel, Sucaldito was rushed to Philippine Heart Center on Sunday morning following an “incident” at his Quezon City residence.

He was pronounced dead at around 10:30 am.

Sucaldito was hospitalized in July after suffering from anxiety and sleep deprivation for nearly a month.

He recovered and returned to hosting OOTD, even recording a near-hour-long episode with Manansala two days before his death.

“The family is still awaiting the official medical findings regarding the cause of his passing,” read another statement from the OOTD Jobert and Chaps Channel.

“We kindly ask everyone to offer prayers for the eternal repose of Nanay Jobert’s soul and to respect the family’s privacy during this difficult time.”

Born on April 16, 1961, Sucaldito worked across various media platforms, including television, radio, and print.

He served as a presenter on the ABS-CBN entertainment talk show The Buzz and anchored his own radio program, Show Buzz, on DZMM.

Sucaldito was also a columnist for Inquirer Bandera.

One of the most recognizable figures in Philippine entertainment media, Sucaldito dabbled in films as well, taking on various roles as producer, publicist, and press coordinator. – Rappler.com

World.title: How second chances led Gwendoline Soriano to the BBP International title
World.content:
Even when circumstances beyond her control forced Baguio's Gwendoline Soriano to withdraw from Binibining Pilipinas in 2022, she never let go of that dream. Four years later, it's now her reality.

Elated is the only way to describe the exact moment Baguio City’s Gwendoline Soriano was called on the 2026 Binibining Pilipinas stage.

“I was smiling the whole time,” Soriano said in a Rappler Talk interview with the rest of the top four beauty queens. “I saw the videos, and it’s nice to share that moment with the people I love. My family and friends are there. The people who supported me were all there. And I get to share the stage with my sisters.”

She was the first finalist to be named, and will go on to represent the Philippines in Miss International next year. Perhaps unbeknownst to many, however, this win was a long time coming for Soriano.

Second chances

Soriano was supposed to compete in the 2022 edition of Binibining Pilipinas, but fate had other plans for her.

Still, she knew that it was a dream worth chasing. Binibining Pilipinas was a pageant she had grown up watching, and it’s where many of the inspiring women she looked up to were molded.

“When I grew up, I realized this is also the path that is for me, and I see it as a calling. And when I had the opportunity to join in 2022, I really tried, but that wasn’t the time for me. I had to go through a lot that time. I had to withdraw because of some conflicts with my work,” she shared.

The universe has a strange way of making you wait for things that aren’t meant for you yet. Disappointment had naturally seeped in when circumstances beyond her control held her back from pursuing this long-time dream. But rather than taking it as a sign to give up completely, she used it to come back even stronger.

In 2025, she entered her first-ever national pageant: Miss Universe Philippines. She placed in the top 12, but Soriano knew she had unfinished business. And so, four whole years after what was supposed to have been her first Binibining Pilipinas stint, she decided to try one more time.

“After four years of waiting and molding and transformation, I believe that this year was really the time for me. Because when the opportunity [arose], I just knew deep in my heart that I had to try again,” Soriano beamed.

The Soriano that walked down the 2026 Binibining Pilipinas stage was not the same one the Philippines witnessed last year. Now 27, the Baguio native is more in tune with who she really is — and this is what she used to win the crown.

“It was my priority to take care of my mind, my body, my soul. Spiritually, most especially, I really have to focus on what really matters,” she shared. “[Before], there were a lot of voices that I had to listen to. And I made sure that I learned from it, and that if I were to try again, I have to know who I really am and what I want. And I have to be firm with my identity, that no matter how loud the noises are, I won’t be listening. Because I am rooted in my identity in Christ.”

A deeply personal advocacy

That Soriano is now the titleholder of Miss International Philippines 2026 is not even the most interesting thing about her.

As a beauty queen, one of your most defining traits is the advocacy that you will choose to spotlight throughout your reign. It’s not something that comes out of nowhere, and Soriano has a personal connection to the cause she champions: Filipino culture and the arts.

The 27-year-old stunner had grown up performing Philippine folk dances, and had naturally carried that interest over to adulthood — having later joined her university’s dance group to hone in on that.

Even when she was just a candidate for Miss Baguio, it had only felt natural for her to focus on an advocacy that ties in with Baguio’s billing as a cultural city. As a dancer herself, it felt like the right choice. Since then, she hasn’t looked back.

Play Video

“It started when I was a candidate for Miss Baguio. We were trying to develop an advocacy that is really close also to our advocacies in Baguio, and we are a cultural city. And that’s something that I also want to integrate to the whole Philippines — that we can shine and express ourselves through creative expression, which is performing arts,” she told Rappler.

Soriano’s passion for this advocacy is also rooted in her lamentation that the youth nowadays have seemed to lose touch with Filipino culture. Even common folk dances like tinikling might get you confused looks in return.

“Other kids don’t know about tinikling anymore. We have a lot of beautiful dances that I really want people to see, especially those abroad. Just so they’d see the beauty of our country, na hindi lang tayo basta-basta resilient, masipag (that we aren’t just resilient and hardworking). We’re not just hardworking and kind people. We have so much to offer. And one part of that is our culture,” Soriano stressed.

But even more than that, Soriano aims to use her Binibining Pilipinas platform to show that pageantry isn’t just about winning titles. It serves a bigger purpose: for beauty queens like Soriano to work on and speak about the issues that really matter.

“We’ve been doing media rounds for a week already and we’re given the chance to talk. To talk about things that matter to us and our opinions on what we should do, on our advocacies, on charities, on even social matters and social news. So, this is why we’re here,” Soriano shared.

“And a lot of people are still celebrating pageantry, especially Binibining Pilipinas. When we were there on the coronation night, that’s what I was thinking about the whole night. Like, ‘Wow, we have a lot of audiences. A lot of people are celebrating this platform.’ And maybe it’s because they know that this is still essential now. This is still a powerful tool for us to speak about our causes and for us to empower the youth and the children and everyone watching us,” she added.

As early as now, it’s clear that Soriano isn’t putting this opportunity to waste. She is well aware that being Binibining Pilipinas International is a responsibility more than just being a title she had fought hard to win. And with that, she’ll strive to make the nation proud. – Rappler.com

World.title: Dozens of OFWs in Dubai seek help to track down Filipino ‘scammer’
World.content:
DUBAI. A general view of the Dubai skyline in the United Arab Emirates, with the Burj Khalifa visible in the center, March 6, 2026.

After gaining people's trust, the alleged scammer would supposedly present a proposal asking for money to fund airline tickets of nonexistent passengers, promising higher returns

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Around 70 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) have banded together to go after a fellow Filipino who allegedly scammed them of a still undetermined amount through a modus involving the supposed purchase of airline tickets.

According to the victims, a certain Joash Meil Calderon, supposedly an employee of an airline company, introduced himself as PJ and befriended them.

Calderon would sell them legitimate airline tickets at cheaper rates to gain trust, at times with benefits like visas and hotel stays in another country. He also issued blank bank checks to bolster confidence.

To target more people, Calderon would introduce himself to the victims’ acquaintances, based on the victims’ accounts. He would also shy away from selfies.

After gaining their trust, Calderon would then allegedly present a proposal asking for money to fund airline tickets of nonexistent passengers, whose Dubai flights he was supposedly arranging through a tour company he was running.

The victims paid from AED25,000 to AED160,000 (P417,000 to P2.67 million), channeled through a bank account. They were supposed to get higher returns for helping Calderon buy the airline tickets, but he just vanished after receiving the money, said the victims.

The alleged scamming happened in a span of four months starting March. According to the victims, Calderon and an accomplice left Dubai for Manila on July 11.

‘Hard-earned money’ gone in an instant

Maria Serna*, 47, reported losing AED160,000 to Calderon. She met him through a friend who bought an airline ticket from him. He supposedly told her that groups of people were coming to Dubai from the Philippines in June and December — the nonexistent passengers.

“It’s hard-earned money. We’re far away from our families, and with all the pressures of work, the money was lost just like that,” said Serna in a mix of English and Filipino. “I no longer hope that my money would be returned, but I want him to be stopped so that no one else will be victimized.”

Another victim, Rhea Ann Fuentes*, claimed she first bought tickets from Calderon in March then was scammed in June.

“He said he was going to book a ticket. But he didn’t have enough money, so he borrowed from us and promised to return our money the next day, with a profit of AED1,000. A portion of the money we gave him was a loan from our in-laws, and we borrowed from a lending company, which we’re still paying off,” Fuentes said in a mix of English and Filipino.

Arman Ibarra lost almost AED24,000 to Calderon, whom he came to know through a colleague, who also later on turned out to be a victim. He described Calderon as “convincing,” with a “calm and kind” tone.

“We want our money back. Otherwise, we’d take legal action,” Ibarra said.

Calderon’s mother reportedly works in Dubai as well. Rappler attempted to contact her, but she shut her Facebook account. A mutual friend tried to reach her on the phone, but she was not taking calls either.

Labor Attaché John Rio Bautista urged the victims to seek assistance from the in-house lawyer of the Migrant Workers Office in Dubai, aside from reporting the matter to police.

“We can issue an advisory, although we have previously issued one asking people to be careful in dealing with possible scams,” Bautista also told Rappler. – Rappler.com

*Names have been changed to protect the identities of the victims.

World.title: Better than before, Eala eyes redemption vs Pegula with Washington title at stake
World.content:
In pursuit of continuous personal growth, Alex Eala hopes her progress translates into a breakthrough crown when she tangles with world No. 3 Jessica Pegula in the Washington Open final

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala needs no extra motivation as she vies for her first-ever WTA Tour crown against Jessica Pegula.

In pursuit of continuous personal growth, Eala hopes her progress translates into a breakthrough crown when she tangles with the world No. 3 American in the final of the Washington Open in the United States on Sunday, August 2 (Monday, August 3, Manila time).

“I still have so much motivation to become a better player, become a better person. I’m 21, so it’s not like I’m the queen of the world or anything,” Eala told Tennis Channel when asked about her “rockstar” status on tour, with large crowds of supporters now a familiar sight at her matches.

“I think another thing is that tennis is such a humbling sport. Another thing is I look back at how far I’ve come or where I come from, and I’ve come a long way.”

Eala has indeed made remarkable strides, reaching her first WTA 500 final and earning another shot at a maiden tour-level title after falling heartbreakingly short in the 2025 Eastbourne Open.

But overcoming Pegula is no easy feat: Pegula already beat Eala before.

It was Pegula who prevented Eala from extending her magical run in the 2025 Miami Open, the American outlasting the Filipina in three sets in the semifinal of the WTA 1000 tournament.

Pegula, whose billionaire parents Terry and Kim Pegula own NFL team Buffalo Bills, has won a pair of titles this year after conquering the WTA 1000 Dubai Tennis Championships and the WTA 500 Charleston Open.

Eala believes she has improved since her last meeting with Pegula, but she understands the daunting task ahead.

“I think, I would say, if I compare myself now to then, I’m more well-rounded. I think I’m physically a little better,” Eala said. “I would say that everything, all the aspects have kind of improved at the same pace.”

“But then again, each player is always evolving and improvement is not a linear thing. Every match is different and I’m sure Jess has also changed so much in these 18 months so it’s going to be great.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Wondering Where to Go in Mangystau This Summer? Start With These Ten Places
World.content:
ASTANA – From canyons and chalk-white cliffs to underground mosques and windswept Caspian shores, Kazakhstan’s Mangystau Region offers some of the country’s most striking landscapes and a growing draw for summer travelers seeking culture, adventure and the unexpected.

Stretching from the shores of the Caspian Sea to the vast Ustyurt Plateau, Mangystau is home to some of Kazakhstan’s most distinctive geological formations. Much of the region was submerged beneath the ancient Tethys Ocean millions of years ago, leaving behind chalk cliffs, colorful canyons, salt flats and fossil-rich landscapes that continue to attract geologists, photographers and adventure travelers from around the world.

Leading the list is Bozzhyra, one of Kazakhstan’s best-known natural landmarks. Located on the Ustyurt Plateau around 300 kilometers from Aktau, the valley is famous for its towering white limestone cliffs and dramatic rock formations shaped by millions of years of erosion. Visitors can explore panoramic viewpoints, hike through the surrounding terrain or join off-road jeep expeditions to experience one of Central Asia’s most spectacular desert landscapes.

Another geological wonder is Torysh, commonly known as the Valley of Balls. Hundreds of perfectly rounded stone spheres, some measuring several meters in diameter, are scattered across the steppe. Scientists believe the formations developed naturally through the cementation of mineral sediments, although local folklore has long surrounded the mysterious stones with legends.

The Airakty–Shomanai Mountains, often nicknamed the Valley of Castles, feature weathered cliffs and rock towers that resemble ancient fortresses. The mountains were formed from limestone deposits on the floor of the ancient Tethys Ocean some 40 million years ago. Tectonic shifts later pushed the terrain upward as the sea retreated, exposing layers of rock that wind and rain gradually shaped into the striking formations seen today. The site is particularly popular among photographers and travelers seeking panoramic views of Mangystau’s rugged terrain.

For those looking to explore more remote landscapes, the Karynzharyk Depression offers one of the region’s most striking panoramas. Its lowest point lies around 75 meters below sea level. At its heart is the Kenderli salt flat, which dries into a cracked white plain in summer but can turn into a mirror-like expanse after rainfall. The area is especially popular for camping, jeep tours and sunrise or sunset photography.

Nature lovers can also visit Tamshaly, a small oasis where freshwater springs trickle down rocky cliffs, creating lush vegetation in the middle of the arid steppe. It is located on the Tupkaragan Peninsula near Fort Shevchenko, around 130 kilometres from Aktau. The shaded gorge provides a welcome retreat from the summer heat and has become a favorite destination for picnics, short hikes and family outings.

The Mangystau Region is also Kazakhstan’s gateway to the Caspian Sea. The beaches of Aktau attract thousands of visitors every summer with sandy shores, modern resorts and a wide range of recreational activities, including swimming, boating, jet skiing and paddleboarding. The city’s waterfront promenade has become one of the country’s most popular seaside leisure destinations.

Alongside its natural attractions, the region is home to important cultural and religious heritage sites. The Beket-Ata Underground Mosque, carved into limestone in the 18th century, remains one of Kazakhstan’s most significant pilgrimage destinations. Built by the revered Sufi scholar Beket-Ata, the mosque welcomes thousands of pilgrims and tourists annually who come to learn about the country’s spiritual traditions while admiring the unique underground architecture.

Among the Mangystau Region’s most recognizable geological monuments is Bokty Mountain, whose nearly symmetrical conical shape resembles a giant yurt rising from the surrounding plains. The 165-meter-high isolated formation also resembles a pyramid from one angle and an overturned ship from another. Located in Mangystau Region’s Karakiya District, Bokty is a state-protected natural monument. The nearest city Zhanaozen is around 90 kilometers away, while the mountain lies roughly 20 kilometers from the unpaved road linking Zhanaozen with the Beket-Ata mosque. Layers of red, yellow and white sedimentary rock create striking patterns that become especially vivid during sunrise and sunset, making the mountain a favorite stop for photographers.

The region’s spectacular scenery continues at Tuzbair, a vast salt flat bordered by towering white chalk escarpments, located around 270 kilometers northeast of Aktau. Formed when the ancient Tethys Ocean retreated millions of years ago, Tuzbair offers visitors dramatic landscapes unlike anywhere else in Kazakhstan. Off-road expeditions, eco-tourism, camping and landscape photography are among the area’s most popular activities.

Completing the list is Kyzylkup, widely known as the Tiramisu Canyon because of its distinctive layers of red, white and golden sedimentary rock that resemble the famous Italian dessert. It is located around 20 kilometers from Bozzhyra and right near the Bokty Mountains. The colorful hills, created through millions of years of geological processes, have become one of the country’s most photographed natural attractions and are increasingly featured in international travel publications. The site is located around 300 kilometers from Aktau. Much of the route follows paved roads, but the section beyond Zhanaozen is unpaved and can be loose or slippery.

With its combination of spectacular natural monuments, ancient spiritual sites and the country’s only Caspian Sea coastline, the Mangystau Region offers visitors an opportunity to experience one of Central Asia’s most diverse and remarkable landscapes, making it an increasingly popular choice for summer travel.

Aktau city is the main gateway and it can be reached by air from major cities in Kazakhstan, including Astana and Almaty, and from abroad, as well as by train and long-distance road connections. While some attractions are accessible on day trips from Aktau, many of Mangystau’s best-known sites lie hundreds of kilometers apart in remote desert terrain. Roads are often unpaved or may be absent altogether, making a high-clearance four-wheel-drive vehicle essential for most routes. Travelers without substantial off-road experience are often advised to join an organized tour or hire a local guide and driver rather than undertake the journey independently.

World.title: Kazakhstan Prepares for First Wild Tiger Release as Reintroduction Project Enters Defining Stage
World.content:
ALMATY – After years of habitat restoration and careful adaptation, the success of Kazakhstan’s tiger restoration effort will soon depend on whether the animals can survive and coexist with people in the wild.

For nearly a decade, Kazakhstan’s effort to restore tigers to the Ili-Balkhash ecosystem has been approaching what conservationists consider its most consequential milestone: the first release of adult Amur tigers into the wild.

According to the Kazakh Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources, two adult tigers transferred from Russia are expected to be released within the next month if they successfully complete the final stage of behavioral assessment. The animals are undergoing tests designed to determine whether they can hunt independently while maintaining a natural avoidance of humans as these two conditions are considered essential for successful reintroduction.

From importing tigers to rebuilding an ecosystem

The planned release represents the transition from years of preparation to the practical implementation of one of Central Asia’s most ambitious wildlife restoration projects.

Rather than focusing solely on breeding or transporting animals, Kazakhstan has invested heavily in recreating the ecological conditions necessary for a self-sustaining tiger population. This has included expanding the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve, restoring prey populations, strengthening environmental protection measures and preparing local communities for coexistence with large predators.

According to the ministry, the reserve now covers more than 450,000 hectares after its expansion earlier this year, creating additional habitat for the future population.

The broader goal extends beyond introducing Amur tigers. Kazakhstan ultimately seeks to restore the ecological niche once occupied by the extinct Caspian (Turanian) tiger, which disappeared from the region in the mid-20th century.

The final test before freedom

Veterinarians and wildlife specialists are assessing whether the adult tigers can consistently hunt live prey while avoiding human interaction. According to the ministry, both animals remain in good physical condition and have demonstrated behavior consistent with wild predators.

Importantly, the tigers continue to avoid people when approached, while direct human contact throughout the adaptation period has been deliberately minimized. Feeding is conducted remotely to ensure the animals never associate humans with food.

“If the current positive results are maintained and the final stages of the assessment are successfully completed, the release may take place in the next month. However, the exact date will be determined only after all the necessary procedures have been completed and the relevant expert opinions have been received,” the ministry told the Kazinform news agency in a written response.

Conservation success depends on local communities

For wildlife experts, releasing the tigers is only half the challenge. Long-term success depends equally on preventing conflict between predators and nearby communities. Recognizing this, Kazakhstan has developed an extensive conflict-prevention system before the first release takes place.

Every released tiger will carry satellite and radio collars allowing specialists to monitor movements around the clock. A dedicated anti-conflict team has already been established within the reserve to respond should an animal approach populated areas.

Perhaps the most notable measure is a new early-warning system. Local residents will receive individual notifications whenever a tiger approaches within five kilometers of a settlement or residence. A dedicated hotline has also been operating since May 2025.

Authorities have also established a livestock compensation mechanism supported by international partners. If a tiger attacks domestic animals, owners will be compensated through a specially created compensation herd, reducing the financial burden on local communities and lowering incentives for retaliation against predators.

Building a population

The two adults expected to be released are part of a larger reintroduction effort. The reserve currently houses six Amur tigers undergoing various stages of adaptation. Two adult and two juvenile animals were transferred from Russia in 2026, while another pair arrived from the Netherlands in 2024.

According to the ministry, all six remain in good health, with the younger animals continuing to develop normally while adapting to their new environment. The staggered introduction reflects international best practice, allowing scientists to monitor each phase before expanding the wild population.

For Kazakhstan, the anticipated release represents more than a conservation milestone as it is the point at which years of planning give way to real-world testing. When Olzhabek Kholov, then a lead expert at the Forestry and Wildlife Committee, told The Astana Times in 2022 that wild tigers could return to Kazakhstan within a few years, the focus was on habitat restoration, prey recovery and international cooperation. Those preparatory stages are largely complete. The next phase will determine whether the country’s long-term investment in ecosystem restoration can translate into a viable wild tiger population.

Whether the project succeeds will ultimately be measured not by the release itself, but by whether the animals establish territories, reproduce naturally and coexist sustainably with surrounding communities.

The coming months will therefore mark the beginning of the project’s most closely watched and scientifically significant phase.

World.title: Kazakhstan Rejects Reports of Complete CPC Shutdown
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry said a complete shutdown of the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) is not under consideration, dismissing media reports suggesting the pipeline’s operations could be fully suspended.

In a statement issued Aug. 1, the ministry said the CPC temporarily suspended operations on July 31 but continues to receive crude oil from shippers and store it in its tank facilities.

Beginning Aug. 1, the CPC resumed accepting around 100,000 metric tons of crude oil per day. Further increases in transportation volumes will depend on the timely arrival of tankers for loading at the consortium’s marine terminal.

The ministry remains in close coordination with the CPC and oil shippers and is closely monitoring the situation.

As pressure on traditional export routes grows, alternative corridors are becoming increasingly important for strengthening the country’s export resilience.

World.title: How Kazakh Youth Transforms Accessibility Through Technology
World.content:
ASTANA – What began as a series of independent projects has grown into Kazakhstan’s first inclusive digital ecosystem, combining transportation, accessibility and communication services into a single platform designed by and for people with disabilities.

Developed by Pavlodar-based university students Stanislav Kirichenko and Islam Kulenov, Involve aims to simplify everyday life through digital solutions that address challenges often overlooked by mainstream technology. The platform brings together services ranging from an accessible taxi booking application and an interactive accessibility map to interface customization tools and AI-powered communication features.

For Kirichenko, the project is deeply personal.

A second-year computer science student at Toraighyrov University in Pavlodar, Kirichenko has lived with a first-group disability since childhood. His interest in programming began while he was still in school, eventually leading him to develop digital tools tailored to the needs of people with disabilities. After meeting Kulenov at university, the two combined their ideas and began building a broader ecosystem to make everyday services more accessible.

In an interview with The Astana Times, the developers said the platform grew directly from their own experiences navigating a world that often fails to consider the needs of people with disabilities.

“Our projects grew out of personal experience. I know firsthand the challenges people with disabilities face every day. Digital services are often difficult to use because of overloaded interfaces and poor accessibility. The problem is not always the lack of solutions, but that they are often designed without involving the people who actually use them,” Kirichenko said.

Before launching Involve, Kirichenko had developed several prototypes, including InvLove, an inclusive social networking and dating platform designed specifically for people with disabilities.

Unlike conventional messaging applications, InvLove adapts to users’ individual needs. People with cerebral palsy, for example, can convert speech into clear text, while users with visual impairments or limited hand mobility can customize the interface or navigate the platform using voice commands.

“It is both a messenger and a dating platform where people with disabilities can communicate, meet new people and, if they want, find a partner or simply make friends,” Kirichenko said.

Kulenov said each founder initially worked on separate accessibility projects before realizing they could achieve greater impact by combining them into one integrated platform.

“We decided to unite everything into a single ecosystem. Our goal was to create one place where users could access all the services they need, much like a super app,” he said.

Building practical solutions for everyday challenges

One of the first products to emerge from the Involve ecosystem was HandyApp, a ride-hailing service designed for people with disabilities.

“Every time I needed an accessible taxi, I had to call a dispatcher, explain my route and wait for confirmation. The process was slow and inconvenient. I kept asking myself why ordering an accessible taxi could not be as simple as booking a regular ride,” Kirichenko said.

That question led the team to develop an application that allows users to request accessible transportation directly from their smartphones, without contacting a dispatcher. Users enter their destination and specify any accessibility requirements before being matched with participating transportation providers.

The developers partnered with several local carriers before launching a pilot program in Aksu city in the Pavlodar Region last year. The four-month trial, conducted from April through July, generated about 720 ride requests through the application.

“The pilot showed there was real demand for this type of service. We are now launching the platform in Pavlodar, where interest has also been high,” Kulenov said.

According to the Pavlodar regional administration, more than 30,000 people with disabilities live in the region, including about 4,200 children. More than 6,800 residents receive specialized social services.

Beyond transportation, the team is developing OpenWays, an interactive accessibility map designed to help people evaluate public buildings before visiting them.

Users can select a location on the map to view detailed accessibility information, including the availability of ramps, elevators, tactile paving, accessible restrooms, platform lifts and doorway dimensions.

“A person can check whether a building is actually accessible before leaving home. The application provides practical information about the environment rather than simply indicating a location,” Kulenov said.

Creating such a platform, however, requires extensive fieldwork.

Kirichenko said the team is currently collecting and verifying accessibility data across urban infrastructure, a process he describes as one of the project’s biggest challenges.

Another component of the ecosystem, OpenU, is designed to make websites and mobile applications more accessible by allowing users to customize digital interfaces according to their individual needs.

The software enables users to adjust font size and typography, disable unnecessary images, switch to high-contrast color themes and navigate applications using voice commands. It is also intended to support people with color blindness and other visual impairments through personalized display settings.

“We want users to be able to adapt any interface to their own needs instead of adapting themselves to the technology,” Kirichenko said.

From startup to national initiative

As Involve has expanded, the project has attracted growing support from the country’s technology community, investors and government institutions.

During an April government meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on implementing Kazakhstan’s Inclusive Policy Concept through 2030, officials identified digital accessibility as a priority. Bektenov instructed relevant ministries to introduce a nationwide application for booking accessible taxis, paving the way for broader deployment of services like HandyApp nationwide.

After graduation, they plan to continue expanding the Involve ecosystem, introduce new digital services and eventually enter international markets.

“We want to keep developing products that genuinely improve people’s quality of life. Our goal is to build sustainable partnerships so the products remain accessible to the people who need them most,” Kulenov said.

World.title: Kazakh Cinema Expands International Festival Presence With San Sebastián Selection
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan continues to strengthen its presence on the international festival circuit as “Mūğalım” (Teacher), the feature debut of director Ayana Nurdinova, has been selected for the New Directors competition at the 74th San Sebastián International Film Festival, one of the world’s oldest and most prestigious Class A festivals in Spain.

“Mūğalım” becomes the first Kazakh film directed by a woman to compete at San Sebastián, marking an important milestone for the country’s film industry as a new generation of filmmakers gains international visibility.

The festival will take place in Spain from Sept. 18 to 26. Its New Directors section is dedicated to first and second feature films, serving as one of the industry’s most respected platforms for emerging directors.

More than a festival selection

Commissioned by the Kazakh Ministry of Culture and Information and supported by the State Center for Support of National Cinema, “Mūğalım” follows a music teacher in the industrial city of Balkhash who dreams of moving to a larger city. When the opportunity finally arrives, he is forced to confront a more profound question: what matters more – the art within him or his place within the world of art?

While the film tells an intimate story about personal ambition and artistic purpose, its selection also reflects broader changes in Kazakhstan’s cinema. Over the past decade, Kazakh productions have increasingly appeared at leading international festivals, signaling growing confidence in the country’s independent and auteur filmmaking.

Why San Sebastián matters

Recognition at San Sebastián carries particular weight. Alongside Cannes, Berlin and Venice, the festival is considered one of the world’s leading Class A film festivals and has long been recognized for discovering influential directors early in their careers.

The New Directors competition has previously introduced audiences to filmmakers who later achieved global acclaim, including Oscar-winning South Korean director Bong Joon Ho. The festival has also played an important role in the careers of Roman Polanski, Francis Ford Coppola and Pedro Almodóvar.

Its history includes landmark premieres such as Alfred Hitchcock’s “North by Northwest” and the European premiere of George Lucas’ “Star Wars,” underscoring its longstanding influence on world cinema.

World.title: With Azerbaijan, Central Asia Seeks Greater Geopolitical Weight
World.content:
ASTANA – The leaders of Central Asia and Azerbaijan gathered in Cholpon-Ata on July 31 for an informal summit aimed at translating years of improving political ties into practical regional integration, as Azerbaijan expands the grouping’s reach across the Caspian and Kazakhstan pushes for an action plan for a landmark cooperation treaty.

The consultative format brings together Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan to discuss trade, energy, transport corridors, tourism, humanitarian cooperation and regional security. Since its launch in 2018, the five Central Asian states have met annually in an informal format without outside powers, demonstrating their growing readiness and political willingness to address shared challenges on their own terms.

“Over the past eight years, the format has clearly evolved. In 2018, the main priority was to rebuild trust among the countries of the region and restore regular high-level dialogue. That was particularly important after a prolonged period in which many regional issues were addressed primarily through bilateral channels,” said Bauyrzhan Auken, lead expert of the Department of Asian Studies at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, in a comment to The Astana Times.

The meeting in Tashkent in 2025 marked a turning point, as it formally admitted Azerbaijan as a full participant and opened the way for a more ambitious phase of regional cooperation.

At the meeting, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a concrete action plan to implement a regional friendship treaty, formally known as the Treaty of Friendship, Good Neighborliness and Cooperation for the Development of Central Asia in the 21st century.

The document was signed in 2022 by the presidents of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan following the fourth consultative meeting. Tajikistan joined the treaty in August 2025, followed by Turkmenistan in June 2026.

Describing the document as historic, Tokayev stressed it “marks a new stage in strategic partnership” and “establishes a political framework for regional cooperation.”

“I believe the next step should be the practical implementation of the document’s provisions. In this regard, I propose developing and subsequently adopting an action plan with clear benchmarks for our long-term cooperation, aimed at further strengthening friendship and good-neighborly relations, as well as expanding trade, economic, cultural and humanitarian cooperation,” Tokayev said.

“It can be said with confidence that, thanks to growing mutual trust and the consistent development of regional cooperation, Central Asia is now experiencing the most successful period in its modern history,” he added.

The consultative format may be entering a more demanding phase, focused less on declarations and more on delivery.

“Today, the consultative meetings are no longer limited to an exchange of views among leaders. A working system has gradually developed around them, with summit rules, road maps, a Council of National Coordinators and closer cooperation among relevant ministries,” Auken said.

“The main question now is how to give the regional treaty practical substance,” he added.

According to him, Tokayev’s proposal to develop a separate action plan directly addresses that challenge. The aim is to define specific priorities, deadlines and responsible agencies. The consultative meetings can therefore now be viewed as a mechanism for setting a common agenda in trade, transport, energy, and investment, among other areas.

Growing trade

This push for closer regional cooperation is increasingly supported by trade. According to Yernar Serik, a foreign trade analyst and founder of the Trade Report Telegram channel, Kazakhstan’s trade with its Central Asian neighbors rose 28.9% year on year to a record $4.2 billion in January-May 2026, with exports reaching $3.2 billion.

Uzbekistan alone accounted for more than half of its regional trade. Bilateral trade rose 37.2% to $2.3 billion in January-May.

The region has also become a particularly important market for Kazakh manufacturers, absorbing 40% of the country’s finished-goods exports, excluding re-exports.

Why coordination matters now

“Coordination among the Central Asian countries has become a necessity,” Auken said, noting that disruptions to transport routes and supply chains, energy and price volatility and conflicts beyond the region can quickly produce consequences across Central Asia.

“At the same time, Central Asian countries face shared challenges involving water resources, climate change, food and energy security, and the need to adapt their economies to global technological shifts. Addressing these issues solely at the national level is becoming increasingly difficult. The countries, therefore, need to align their interests, exchange information and jointly plan their next steps,” he explained.

Transport and logistics are also taking on a greater importance in discussions.

“Geopolitical instability has increased the need to diversify routes between Asia and Europe. Developing alternative corridors allows the countries of the region to strengthen the resilience of supply chains and reduce their dependence on individual routes,” he said.

Informal format

According to Auken, the format’s flexibility is its strength. It does not require governments to transfer authority to a supranational body, build a large permanent bureaucracy or surrender elements of national sovereignty.

“It allows leaders to discuss sensitive issues openly, coordinate their positions and advance joint initiatives without excessive bureaucracy,” the expert said.

Auken cautioned that closer coordination does not mean the countries were seeking to build a closed regional bloc or distance themselves from outside partners. Instead, the objective was to align their positions more effectively and defend shared regional interests amid intensifying competition among major powers.

“At the same time, the format’s flexibility does not relieve the countries of the need to implement the agreements they reach. Decisions made at the leaders’ level must be followed through by executive agencies,” he said.

Azerbaijan expands the format across the Caspian

Azerbaijan’s inclusion as a full participant marks a significant expansion of the consultative format beyond Central Asia’s five states. Its participation strengthens the trans-Caspian dimension and creates new opportunities for cooperation in transport, energy, trade and investment. With Azerbaijan serving as a key link to the South Caucasus, Türkiye and European markets, the enlarged format could help advance a more integrated regional transport and logistics network, including the Middle Corridor.

According to Tokayev, Azerbaijan’s inclusion marked a new stage in the format’s evolution.

“Through our joint efforts, we are creating conditions for deeper political dialogue, expanded cooperation in investment, energy and industry, and the development of an integrated transport and logistics system,” he said.

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev reinforced that broader vision, saying Azerbaijan’s accession had elevated the consultative format to a “qualitatively new, macro-regional level.” His remarks pointed to an emerging geopolitical concept that links Central Asia with the South Caucasus and Afghanistan through transport, trade and development ties.

According to Auken, Azerbaijan’s participation does not transform the grouping into a broader political bloc and does not alter the Central Asian character of the format.

“Rather, it gives the grouping greater substance and strengthens its practical dimension. It enables the countries to advance projects whose significance extends across the wider trans-Caspian region,” he said, noting that it creates additional opportunities for Central Asian countries to pursue joint projects in transport, energy and digital infrastructure.

“This is most visible in transport,” he said, stressing that Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan are key actors in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, which links China and Europe through Central Asia, the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus.

“For the countries of the region, developing the corridor offers a way to diversify routes, reduce dependence on individual transit channels and strengthen their position in Eurasian logistics,” Auken said.

He also highlighted opportunities in energy, industry, investment and digital infrastructure.

“One example is the planned fiber-optic cable across the Caspian Sea between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, which is expected to improve regional digital connectivity and create an additional data-transmission route,” said the expert.

Stronger voice of Central Asia

Addressing the meeting, Tokayev said Central Asia’s role in global affairs is steadily growing and that the region’s voice is becoming increasingly prominent on the international stage.

“Kazakhstan remains committed to the agreements reached and will continue advancing constructive initiatives aimed at strengthening friendship, good-neighborly relations and strategic partnership among our countries. I am confident that, through our joint efforts, we will achieve even greater progress,” Tokayev said.

The expanded format does not amount to a closed regional bloc. Instead, it reflects an effort by Central Asian states to coordinate more effectively, reduce their vulnerability to external shocks and approach larger powers with a clearer sense of shared interests.
